Hook: **contact → calcium → consequence.** Ca²⁺ is always in the middle. (Aside: the *fast* block — a membrane depolarization from Na⁺ influx — happens even earlier, but it isn't one of the three ranked steps, so it doesn't change the 1-2-3 order.)

cards.title: The potency ladder: toti > pluri > multi > uni
cards.body:
Potency **narrows** as development proceeds:
- **Totipotent** — whole organism **+ placenta**. Example: the **zygote / early (up to ~8-cell) blastomeres**.
- **Pluripotent** — any body cell but **not** placenta. Examples: **embryonic stem cells** (inner cell mass) and **iPSCs**.
- **Multipotent** — several cell types within **one lineage**. Example: **hemocytoblast** (blood stem cell) → all blood cells, nothing else.
- **Unipotent** — one cell type only (e.g. a committed progenitor).

iPSCs (Yamanaka reprogrammed a **fibroblast**; mouse 2006, human 2007) are **pluripotent** — the 'induced' wording tempts a fancier answer, but they can't make placenta, so not totipotent.

cards.title: Cleavage & determination — two independent axes
cards.body:
**Cleavage completeness** (about yolk):
- **Holoblastic** = complete cleavage (frog, sea urchin, mammal, earthworm — little/moderate yolk).
- **Meroblastic** = partial cleavage; a huge yolk blocks the furrow so only a disc cleaves (**birds**, reptiles, most fish).

**Cell-fate flexibility** (about determination):
- **Mosaic / determinate** — fate fixed early; remove a blastomere → **missing organs**. Type case: **nematodes** (and the classic spiral-cleaving protostomes).
- **Regulative** — remaining cells compensate → normal embryo (or twins). Type cases: **echinoderms & chordates** (vertebrates).

Don't conflate the axes: 'meroblastic' is about yolk, 'mosaic' is about fate. Mammals are holoblastic **and** regulative; birds are meroblastic — the two labels are set by different things.

cards.title: Buzz words → instant answer
cards.body:
- "arrested / stage of meiosis right before fertilization" → **metaphase II**
- "acrosomal... cortical granules... rank the steps" → **bind → Ca²⁺ → cortical reaction**
- "induced a fibroblast into a stem cell / Yamanaka" → **pluripotent (iPSC)**
- "hemocytoblast / blood stem cell" → **multipotent**
- "yolk-rich / incomplete cleavage / birds" → **meroblastic**
- "remove one blastomere → missing organs" → **mosaic/determinate → nematode**
- "primitive streak lengthens and narrows" → **convergent extension**
- "Sertoli cells / anti-Müllerian hormone" → Müllerian = **female** tract
- "unfertilized egg / apomixis in animals" → **parthenogenesis**
- "neural tube not closed / spina bifida" → **folic acid (B9 / folate)**

cards.title: Worked buzz: the 4-cell removal question
cards.body:
**Clue:** "Removes one of 4 cells; the adult is **missing major organs**. Which phyla could this be — Echinodermata, Chordata, Nematoda?"

**Read it:** 'lose a cell → lose its organs' is the signature of **mosaic / determinate** development, where each blastomere's fate is fixed early and no neighbor can replace it. Echinoderms and chordates are **regulative** (they compensate — that's why you can split a sea-urchin or mammalian embryo and get twins). Only **nematodes** are mosaic.

**Land it: 3 only (Nematoda).** The trap is picking the vertebrate/echinoderm because they're 'famous' embryos — but famous *because* they regulate, the opposite of what the clue describes.

cards.title: Gastrulation movement — convergent extension
cards.body:
The **lengthening and narrowing of the primitive streak** (and the elongating body axis) during gastrulation is driven by **convergent extension**: cells **intercalate** between neighbors along one axis, so the tissue gets **longer and thinner** — literally 'converge (narrow) + extend (lengthen).'

Keep the four movements straight:
- **Convergent extension** — cells slot between each other → tissue elongates.
- **Invagination** — a sheet infolds (buckles inward).
- **Ingression** — individual cells detach from a sheet and migrate inward.
- **Involution** — a sheet rolls inward over an edge/lip.

cards.title: Sex-tract determination: AMH and the two duct systems
cards.body:
Two duct systems start in every embryo:
- **Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts → female** tract (uterus, oviducts, upper vagina).
- **Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts → male** tract (epididymis, vas deferens), maintained by **testosterone** from **Leydig cells**.

In a normal XY embryo, **Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)**, which **causes the Müllerian (female) ducts to regress**. **Female is the default** duct fate — the male program must actively suppress it.

So **malfunctioning Sertoli cells → no AMH → Müllerian ducts persist**, while Leydig-cell testosterone still builds the Wolffian tract → the baby develops **both** a female and a male reproductive tract.

cards.title: The classic distractor pairs — keep these from flipping
cards.body:
- **Primary oocyte (2n, prophase I) vs secondary oocyte (1n, metaphase II)** — meiosis I is the halving step, so the secondary oocyte and egg are haploid.
- **Meroblastic (partial, yolky — birds) vs holoblastic (complete — frog, urchin, mammal, earthworm).**
- **Mosaic/determinate (nematodes — lose cell, lose organs) vs regulative (echinoderms & chordates — compensate).**
- **Totipotent (zygote/early blastomeres, + placenta) vs pluripotent (ES cells & iPSCs, no placenta).**
- **Incomplete metamorphosis (Orthoptera — no pupa) vs complete (Hymenoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera — larva + pupa).**
- **Determinate growth (animals) vs indeterminate (plants)** — do NOT flip; 'plants undergo determinate growth' is FALSE.

cards.title: Metamorphosis & plant-vs-animal growth — the memory hooks
cards.body:
**Metamorphosis:** if the life cycle has a **maggot/grub/caterpillar larva AND a pupa** stage, it's **complete (holometabolous)** — egg → larva → pupa → adult (bees/ants = Hymenoptera, flies = Diptera, butterflies/moths = Lepidoptera, beetles = Coleoptera). No pupa, just egg → nymph (mini-adult that grows by molts) → adult = **incomplete (hemimetabolous)** — grasshoppers/crickets = **Orthoptera**, roaches, true bugs.

**Plant vs animal:** plants grow **indeterminately** from meristems (juvenile + adult forms can coexist on one body) and elongate throughout life; animals grow **determinately** toward a fixed adult form. Bonus contrasts flip that clause ('plants undergo determinate growth') to bait you — that statement is false; it's animals that are determinate.

memorize.answer: Diploid (2n) — it's the only one still before meiosis I; the secondary oocyte and egg are haploid (1n)
Acrosomal binding → intracellular Ca²⁺ rise → cortical granule fusion (bind → calcium → cortical reaction)
Pluripotent (any body cell, but not placenta)
Multipotent (all blood cells, one lineage only)

memorize.trigger: Remove a blastomere → adult missing organs
memorize.answer: Mosaic/determinate development → Nematoda (not the regulative echinoderms/chordates)
Convergent extension (cells intercalate → tissue longer + thinner)

memorize.trigger: Malfunctioning Sertoli cells / no anti-Müllerian hormone in XY baby
memorize.answer: Both male AND female reproductive tracts develop (Müllerian ducts persist; testosterone still builds the Wolffian tract)

memorize.trigger: Neural tube fails to close / spina bifida cause

practice.note: Straight recall of the second arrest. Don't answer prophase I — that's the primary oocyte before ovulation. The egg awaiting sperm is the secondary oocyte.
practice.solution: Oocytes are arrested at metaphase II right before fertilization; sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II. Correct answer: metaphase II.

practice.note: 'Identify ALL' format — grade each cell individually. Meiosis I is the halving step, so anything after it is haploid.
practice.solution: The primary oocyte is diploid (still before meiosis I). The secondary oocyte and the mature egg are both haploid because meiosis I already separated the homologs. Correct answer: 2 and 3.

practice.note: Ranking question. Use the cause-and-effect chain rather than rote order: sperm must touch before anything else happens, and Ca²⁺ is the middle messenger.
practice.solution: Acrosomal process binds receptors (contact) → intracellular Ca²⁺ rises (signal) → cortical granules fuse (the cortical reaction / slow block to polyspermy). Correct order: 1, 2, 3.

practice.note: 'Identify all multipotent.' Epidermal cells are differentiated (not stem cells); embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, not multipotent — the trap is over-ranking them.
practice.solution: Only the hemocytoblast (hematopoietic stem cell) is multipotent — it makes all blood cell types but nothing outside that lineage. Epidermal cells aren't stem cells; ES cells are pluripotent. Correct answer: 3 only.

practice.note: 'Lose a cell → lose organs' = mosaic/determinate. The bait is the two famous regulative embryos (echinoderm, chordate); pick the odd one out.
practice.solution: Removing a blastomere and getting a defective adult only happens in mosaic/determinate developers. Echinoderms and chordates are regulative (they compensate), so only Nematoda fits. Correct answer: 3 only.

practice.note: Track the two duct systems separately. No AMH doesn't feminize — testosterone is still present, so the male tract still forms while the female tract fails to regress.
practice.solution: Sertoli cells normally make anti-Müllerian hormone, which makes the Müllerian (female) ducts regress. Without AMH those ducts persist, but Leydig-cell testosterone still builds the Wolffian (male) tract — so the baby develops both female and male reproductive tracts. Correct answer: Y.

subject: bio

why: Cell biology is the single densest and most frequently tested bio topic in the Science Bowl bank (21 questions, ~6% share). Nearly every question is a distinction or a count that a handful of memorized rules solve instantly, so it has the best points-per-study-hour in biology.
overview:
## Cell Biology — the eukaryotic cell as a machine

This topic covers the plasma membrane, the organelles, vesicle traffic, the cytoskeleton, cell junctions, and the signaling that ties them together. It is the **single densest bio topic** in the bank — worth mastering because the questions cluster tightly around a few repeated patterns.

**How it shows up.** The writers almost never ask a raw definition. They ask you to *apply a rule under time pressure*, in one of four molds:
- **Rank / "which diffuses fastest"** through a bilayer → permeability rule.
- **"How many membranes / bilayers"** does X cross → count the route.
- **"Which coat / junction / organelle / signaling class"** does Y → a lookup map.
- **Stacked traps** — two concepts in one stem (FRAP *and* FRET, cyclin *vs* collagen, peroxisome *vs* lysosome).

**Smartest way to learn it.** Do **not** memorize organelles as a flat list. Learn the five *rules that generate the answers*:
1. **Permeability:** small + nonpolar wins ($CO_2$ > $H_2O$ > glucose > ions).
2. **Fluidity:** cold → shorten tails / add double bonds; cholesterol is a *buffer*.
3. **Membrane count:** walk the bus through and tally bilayers (mito 2, chloroplast 2, nucleus 2, +1 per engulfment).
4. **Vesicle coats:** COPII out (ER→Golgi), COPI back (Golgi→ER, KDEL retrieval), clathrin to the cell surface / endosome.
5. **Junction map:** gap = connexins, tight = claudin/occludin, adherens = cadherin+actin, desmosome = cadherin+keratin.

Master those five and roughly 15 of the 21 questions fall on sight. Every fact below carries a *why* so it sticks — bio is recall-heavy, and a mechanism you understand survives the buzzer better than a fact you crammed.

cards.title: The permeability rule: nonpolar > small polar > large polar > ions
cards.body:
A phospholipid bilayer's hydrophobic core **rejects charge first, then size.** So the crossing speed order is:

$CO_2$ (small, nonpolar — sails through) **>** $H_2O$ (small but polar — slips through slowly on its own; in real cells aquaporins speed it up) **>** glucose (large polar — needs a transporter) **>** $Cl^-$ / $Na^+$ (charged, drag a hydration shell — need channels/pumps).

**WHY water still beats glucose/ions despite being polar:** it is tiny and uncharged, so it can transiently slip between lipid tails; a hydrated ion is effectively huge and its charge is repelled outright. The one hook that wins two different questions: **$CO_2$ (and $O_2$, steroids) always beats water.** Whenever a stem says 'rank... cross a bilayer' or 'diffuse fastest without transporters,' this is the rule.

cards.title: WHY cold membranes need shorter / unsaturated tails (and what cholesterol really does)
cards.body:
Cold makes a membrane **gel up** (lipids pack tight, rigid). To *keep* fluidity you loosen the packing:
- **Shorten** the fatty-acid tails (less surface area to stick together via van der Waals), or
- **Add double bonds** (cis kinks that stop tight packing).

**Cholesterol is a two-way buffer, not a one-way lever:** when it's cold it *raises* fluidity (its rigid ring props lipids apart so they can't crystallize); when it's hot it *lowers* fluidity (it restrains lipid movement). It fights whatever the temperature is doing — so 'add cholesterol' is never the single *best* cold-fix answer. Note the trap distractor 'decrease cholesterol' is actively *wrong* in the cold (you'd remove the thing propping lipids apart); 'shorten tails' is the right answer.

cards.title: WHY the membrane-count method works — walk the bus, tally bilayers
cards.body:
Every organelle boundary you physically pierce is one bilayer. Don't recall a number — **draw the route and count.**

Memorize the base counts: mitochondrion = **2** (inner + outer), chloroplast = **2** (+ thylakoid = a 3rd), nucleus = **2** (continuous with the ER). **Phagocytosis adds +1** (the phagosome membrane) on top of the target's own plasma membrane.

Worked (a real bank item): protist-mito inside a macrophage → mito inner+outer (2) + protist plasma membrane (1) + macrophage phagosome membrane (1) + macrophage plasma membrane (1) = **5**. Second drill: thylakoid lumen → nucleoplasm = thylakoid membrane (1) + 2 chloroplast envelope (2) + 2 nuclear envelope (2) = **5**. Both '5' answers come from *walking the path*, not memorizing.

cards.title: Vesicle coat map: COPII out, COPI back, clathrin to the surface
cards.body:
Three coats, three directions:
- **COPII = anterograde**, ER → Golgi ('COP-**II** goes **to** the Golgi').
- **COPI = retrograde**, Golgi → ER ('COP-**I** = return'). This is what retrieves **KDEL**-tagged ER-resident escapees back to the ER.
- **Clathrin** = *trans*-Golgi / plasma membrane → endosome (endocytosis, at the cell surface and inward).

Trap phrasing: **'transport *away from* the Golgi'** = COPI (to ER) **and** clathrin (to the cell) — **not** COPII, which moves *toward* the Golgi. KDEL-ordering questions: a KDEL protein that escaped to the Golgi rides **COPI** back to the ER *first*, gets re-folded by a chaperonin in the ER, and only then re-exits on COPII — so the sequence is COPI → chaperonin → COPII.

cards.title: Junction map + the cytoskeleton trio
cards.body:
**Four junctions, know the protein:**
- **Gap** junction = **connexins** (six build one connexon channel; electrical/chemical coupling). *Only* junction that uses connexins.
- **Tight** junction = **claudin / occludin** (seal the paracellular gap).
- **Adherens** = **cadherin + actin**.
- **Desmosome** = **cadherin + keratin** (intermediate filaments — the 'spot welds').

**Cytoskeleton by width:** microfilaments (**actin**, ~7 nm, thinnest) < intermediate filaments (**keratin**, coiled-coil, ~10 nm) < microtubules (**tubulin**, ~25 nm, widest). Keratin's mid-range tensile intermediate filaments are exactly why it anchors **desmosomes** against mechanical stress — and **spectrin** (an actin-linked mesh) is the special one beneath the **RBC** membrane, giving the cell its flexibility.

cards.title: Buzz words → the organelle / class they point to
cards.body:
- **'very-long-chain fatty acid' (>C22, e.g. lignoceric acid), 'a fatty acid too long for the mitochondrion,' 'ROS / superoxide / oxidative (respiratory) burst'** → **peroxisome** (NOT lysosome or mitochondrion). *Fact-check flags the writers gloss over: lignoceric acid is really **C24**, not the 'C26' a stem may state; and the phagocyte respiratory burst is physically run by membrane **NADPH oxidase** — peroxisome is simply the ROS-handling organelle among the answer choices.*
- **'binds a ligand on the *adjacent* cell,' 'Notch'** → **juxtacrine.**
- **'no clathrin' + 'cargo delivered direct to cytosol'** → **potocytosis** (via caveolae).
- **'photobleach + no recovery'** → decreased **fluidity** (FRAP); **'signal rises as two things get close'** → **interaction** (FRET).
- **'highest ubiquitination / degradation rate'** → **cyclin** (timed disposal).
- **'circular chromosome, matrix higher pH than intermembrane space, folds'** → **mitochondrion** (folds = *cristae*).

cards.title: The classic distractor pairs — know which is which
cards.body:
- **Cristae vs cisternae:** cristae = **mitochondria** inner-membrane folds; cisternae = flattened **Golgi/ER** stacks. Swapped-word trap (the bank uses exactly this — 'folds called cisternae' is the false statement).
- **COPI vs COPII:** I returns to the ER (retrograde); II goes to the Golgi (anterograde).
- **Extrinsic vs intrinsic apoptosis:** **Fas ligand / TNF / death receptors = extrinsic** (signal from outside); **cytochrome c / DNA damage / hypoxia = intrinsic** (internal stress, mitochondrial release of cyt c).
- **Peroxisome vs lysosome vs mitochondrion:** ROS/superoxide handling & β-oxidation of >C22 fats = **peroxisome** (its oxidases make $H_2O_2$, catalase clears it); acid-hydrolase digestion = **lysosome**; ATP + β-oxidation of ordinary-length fats = **mitochondrion**.
- **Paracrine vs juxtacrine:** diffuses to a neighbor = paracrine; must physically **touch** the adjacent cell = juxtacrine.
- **Water vs $CO_2$:** nonpolar $CO_2$ is **faster** than polar water across a bare bilayer.

cards.title: WHY cyclins are ubiquitinated most — timing = disposability
cards.body:
The cell cycle only works if its regulators are **destroyed on schedule.** Cyclins are built to be disposable: heavily tagged with ubiquitin (by the APC/C and SCF ligases), short timed half-lives, chewed up by the proteasome right on cue so the next phase can begin.

Contrast with **structural** proteins (collagen) — long-lived, rarely ubiquitinated — and with metabolic enzymes on the answer sheet (phosphofructokinase, protein kinase A), which are stably maintained. The rule: **'the more a protein's job is *timing*, the shorter its half-life.'** So in any 'highest degradation rate' question, pick the cell-cycle regulator over the structural or housekeeping protein.

cards.title: Worked buzz — the stacked FRAP + FRET trap
cards.body:
**Stem:** FRET signal *increases*; then photobleach the membrane and fluorescence *does not fully recover*. Conclusion about the drug-protein complex?

**Land it in two moves:**
1. **FRET rising** = the donor and acceptor fluorophores are within ~10 nm = drug and protein **are interacting.** (FRET measures proximity/interaction.)
2. **No recovery after photobleach (FRAP)** = unbleached molecules aren't diffusing back into the bleached spot = **decreased membrane fluidity.**

Stack them → **'they are interacting AND decreasing membrane fluidity.'** The trap works only if you conflate the two techniques; keep them separate — **FRET = proximity, FRAP = fluidity.**

cards.title: Calcium chelator — what it does NOT disrupt
cards.body:
A calcium chelator (e.g., EGTA) mops up free $Ca^{2+}$, so it disrupts **Ca-dependent** events: fertilization-envelope formation, LTP, neurotransmitter release, smooth-muscle/peristalsis contraction, IP3-driven signaling.

The answer to 'least likely disrupted' is **action-potential *initiation* in a sensory neuron** — that depolarizing upstroke is driven by voltage-gated **$Na^+$** influx, not calcium. Calcium matters at the synapse (vesicle release) downstream, but the AP *initiation/upstroke* itself is sodium-driven. Don't reflexively pick anything with 'neuron' in it — trace which *ion* actually carries the step.

memorize.trigger: Fastest across a bare lipid bilayer (no transporter)
memorize.answer: CO2 (small + nonpolar) — always beats water; O2 and steroids also fast

memorize.trigger: Cold membrane, best way to restore fluidity
memorize.answer: Shorten fatty-acid tails / add double bonds (unsaturate). Cholesterol = buffer, and 'decrease cholesterol' is wrong in the cold
Decreased membrane fluidity (molecules not diffusing back in)
The two molecules are interacting (fluorophores within ~10 nm)
COPI = retrograde Golgi→ER (KDEL return); COPII = anterograde ER→Golgi

memorize.trigger: Coats for transport AWAY from the Golgi
memorize.answer: COPI (to ER) and clathrin (to cell surface/endosome) — NOT COPII

memorize.trigger: KDEL protein escaped to Golgi — order back home
memorize.answer: COPI (retrograde to ER) → chaperonin (refold in ER) → COPII (re-exit)

memorize.trigger: Gap junction protein (only junction using it)
Breakdown of very-long-chain fatty acids (>C22) OR ROS/superoxide/oxidative burst — which organelle?
memorize.answer: Peroxisome (oxidases make H2O2, catalase clears it; β-oxidizes VLCFAs mito can't). Note: lignoceric acid is really C24 not C26; the burst itself is NADPH-oxidase driven
Juxtacrine (ligand on the adjacent cell membrane, contact-dependent)

memorize.trigger: Clathrin-independent endocytosis, cargo delivered direct to cytosol
Highest ubiquitination / degradation rate among proteins
memorize.answer: Cyclin (timed disposal; beats collagen, PFK, PKA)
Extrinsic = Fas ligand / TNF / death receptors; intrinsic = cytochrome c / DNA damage / hypoxia
IP3 (opens ER Ca2+ channels) + DAG (activates PKC)
Cristae = mitochondria; cisternae = Golgi/ER (matrix pH also HIGHER than intermembrane space)

practice.note: 'Diffuse the fastest through a lipid bilayer' — pure permeability rule. Screen out anything charged or large first, then favor small + nonpolar.
practice.solution: Carbon dioxide is small and nonpolar, so it passes straight through the hydrophobic core with no transporter — faster than polar water and far faster than sodium (charged, hydrated) or glucose (large, polar). CO2 is the reflex answer whenever the stem asks 'fastest across a bilayer.'

practice.note: A 'how many bilayers' count. Don't guess — walk the route from the innermost point outward and tally every membrane you cross.
practice.solution: From inside the protist's mitochondrion outward: mito inner + outer membranes (2) → protist's own plasma membrane (1) → macrophage's phagosome membrane that engulfed it (1) → macrophage's plasma membrane (1) = 5. Engulfment adds the +1 phagosome layer that trips people up.

practice.note: 'Away from the Golgi' is the trap phrase. COPII moves TOWARD the Golgi, so it must be excluded; identify the coats that leave it.
practice.solution: Transport away from the Golgi is handled by clathrin-coated vesicles (trans-Golgi → endosome/plasma membrane) and COPI (retrograde, Golgi → ER, e.g. KDEL retrieval). COPII does the opposite direction (ER → Golgi), so the answer is 1 and 2.

practice.note: A KDEL-retrieval ordering puzzle. A KDEL protein that escaped to the Golgi must be shipped BACK to the ER, then folded, then can re-exit. Track the direction at each step.
practice.solution: Starting in the Golgi on a KDEL-tagged protein: COPI (2) is the retrograde coat that grabs the KDEL protein and carries it back to the ER first; once in the ER a chaperonin (1) assists folding; COPII (3) is the anterograde ER→Golgi coat, so it comes last. Order: 2, 1, 3.

practice.note: Junction-protein matching. Only one of the three junction types uses connexins; know that gap junctions are the channel-forming ones.
practice.solution: Connexins assemble into connexons, the channels of gap junctions that electrically/chemically couple cells — so gap junction only (1). Adherens junctions use cadherin+actin; desmosomes use cadherin+keratin. Neither uses connexins.

practice.note: 'Least likely disrupted by a calcium chelator.' Chelators remove free Ca2+, so anything Ca-dependent IS disrupted — find the one process that runs on a different ion.
practice.solution: The action-potential upstroke/initiation in a sensory neuron is driven by voltage-gated Na+ influx, not calcium, so removing Ca2+ doesn't block it. The Ca-dependent events (fertilization-envelope formation, LTP, peristalsis/contraction) would all be disrupted — making AP initiation the correct 'least disrupted' choice.

subject: bio

why: Neuroscience & senses is ~5.5% of Science Bowl bio and is unusually reasoning-friendly: three core pathways (visual pathway, neuron ion story, cholinergic autonomic map) generate most answers, so a small investment converts a big block of questions from guesswork to certainty. Vision/optics alone is a third of the set.
overview:
**What it covers.** Neuron electrophysiology (resting and action potentials, synapses), neurotransmitters and the drugs/toxins that hit them, brain regions, glial cells, and — heavily — the **eye and vision** (roughly a third of the questions).

**How it shows up.** Three flavors dominate:
1. **Ordering questions** — "put these in order by X" (visual pathway, cone density, disorder distance from the retina).
2. **Pharmacology puzzles** — a drug/toxin is described by *mechanism* and you name the target (MAO, adenosine, ACh), or the reverse.
3. **True/false-all membrane traps** — a list where you flag every true statement, and the answer is often "None." These hinge on one precise detail (permeability vs. concentration; all-or-nothing amplitude).

The questions are **mechanism-first**: they tell you what something *does* and want the name.

**Smartest way to learn it.** Don't memorize terms in isolation. Learn **three things cold** and the rest falls out: (a) the **visual pathway in order**, (b) the **ion story** (K⁺ out = more negative; Cl⁻ in = inhibitory), and (c) the **cholinergic autonomic map** (ACh everywhere except the sympathetic final step). Then hang each drug on the pathway it hits. If you can *draw the eye and the neuron*, you reason to answers instead of recalling them — which is exactly what the mechanism-first phrasing rewards.

cards.title: The visual pathway, in order
cards.body:
**Photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve/tract → LGN (thalamus) → visual cortex.**

- Light hits the **back** of the retina first (photoreceptors), then the signal travels *forward* through retinal interneurons before exiting.
- **Ganglion cell axons ARE the optic nerve/tract** — they're the same thing at different points, so an ordering list may separate them but they're one continuous projection.
- The **LGN** (lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus) is the last relay before cortex.

Memory hook: *"Photo-Bi-Gang goes to the Optic LGN."* Any ordering question about retina→brain is just this list.

cards.title: Retinal geography: cones, blind spot, and edge-sharpening
cards.body:
- **Cone density: fovea (max) > outer macula > optic disc (zero).** Fovea = pinpoint of sharpest color/detail, all cones and no rods. Optic disc = where the nerve axons exit and vessels enter = **no photoreceptors = blind spot**.
- **Horizontal cells** perform **lateral inhibition** — they suppress neighboring photoreceptors to sharpen edges/contrast. (Amacrine cells do analogous lateral processing one layer inward, at the bipolar→ganglion synapse.)
- **Disorder distance from the retina (front→back of eye):** conjunctivitis (surface/conjunctiva) is farthest, cataract (lens) is middle, macular degeneration (retina itself) is closest.

cards.title: WHY the resting potential trap works: permeability ≠ concentration
cards.body:
The membrane sits near the equilibrium (Nernst) potential of whatever ion it's **most permeable to** — at rest that's **K⁺** (very negative).

- **↑ K⁺ permeability →** more K⁺ leaves down its gradient → inside gets **more negative** (hyperpolarize). ✓
- **↑ extracellular Cl⁻ →** makes E_Cl more negative and drives Cl⁻ **in** → net negative charge inside → **more negative**. ✓
- **↑ extracellular Na⁺ →** basically nothing at rest, because resting Na⁺ *permeability* is tiny. A concentration change only moves the membrane if a channel for that ion is actually open. ✗

The question deliberately mixes "permeability" and "concentration" words. Separate them and it's easy — the effect scales with permeability, not with the gradient alone.

cards.title: WHY inhibition = chloride: the 'neuron 2 cancels neuron 3' puzzle
cards.body:
An inhibitory neuron makes its target **harder to fire** by opening channels that hyperpolarize or clamp the membrane near threshold:
- **Excitatory (EPSP):** Na⁺ / Ca²⁺ **in** (depolarize toward threshold).
- **Inhibitory (IPSP):** **Cl⁻ in** or **K⁺ out** (drive away from / shunt threshold). GABA and glycine do this via Cl⁻.

So when "neuron 1 alone fires neuron 3, but 1+2 together don't," neuron 2 must be **increasing Cl⁻ permeability** — a fast, per-spike veto. It is NOT LTP/LTD (those are slow changes in synaptic *strength*, not a moment-to-moment cancellation) and NOT opening Na⁺ (that would *help* fire neuron 3).

cards.title: The cholinergic autonomic map
cards.body:
**ACh is the NT at: ALL preganglionic autonomic neurons (sympathetic AND parasympathetic) + ALL parasympathetic postganglionic neurons.**

The main exception is the **sympathetic postganglionic** neuron, which switches to **norepinephrine**.

Hook: *"ACh everywhere except sympathetic's final step."* So any list of autonomic junctions asking "where is ACh the transmitter" is almost always **ALL** of them — unless it explicitly names a sympathetic *post*ganglionic synapse.

(Real-world asterisks that Science Bowl rarely tests: sympathetic postganglionic fibers to **sweat glands** are cholinergic, and the adrenal medulla is innervated directly by a sympathetic *pre*ganglionic — hence cholinergic — fiber.)

cards.title: Buzz words → reflex answers
cards.body:
- **"monoamine oxidase / MAO"** → breaks down the monoamines dopamine, serotonin, NE. *MAO inhibitor* → treats **depression** or **Parkinson's** (raises dopamine).
- **"increased intraocular pressure" / ciliary body overproduces aqueous humor / drainage blocked** → **glaucoma**.
- **"causes drowsiness" + caffeine blocks it** → **adenosine** (caffeine is a competitive adenosine-receptor antagonist).
- **"excitatory NT" + "LTP / learning / memory"** → **glutamate** (via NMDA receptors).
- **"reward / addiction / overreleases dopamine — inhibit which region?"** → **ventral tegmental area (VTA)**.
- **"glial cell from hematopoietic/mesodermal origin"** → **microglia** (brain's resident immune cell).
- **"lateral inhibition / sharpen / deactivate neighbors" in retina** → **horizontal cells**.
- **"thalamus stroke — which sense is spared?"** → **olfaction** (only sense that skips the thalamus).

cards.title: Worked buzz — the STED microscopy question
cards.body:
*Clue:* "STED microscopy deactivates neighboring fluorophores to sharpen an effective spot and beat the diffraction limit. This is similar to which eye cells?"

**How to land it fast:** the load-bearing phrase is **"deactivate neighbors to sharpen."** That is the textbook definition of **lateral inhibition**. In the retina, lateral inhibition is done by **horizontal cells**. You don't need to know STED at all — you translate its mechanism into a retina term and match. Answer: **horizontal cells.** This is the archetype for every "this weird thing is *analogous to* what bio structure?" question — strip it to the mechanism verb and match that, ignoring the jargon.

cards.title: Classic distractor pairs to keep straight
cards.body:
- **Myopia vs. hyperopia:** myopia (nearsighted, eye too *long*, image focuses in *front* of the retina) → fixed by a **concave/biconcave** (diverging) lens. Hyperopia (farsighted, eye too short) → convex (converging). *If a biconcave lens fixes it, it's myopia.*
- **VTA vs. substantia nigra:** both dopaminergic — **VTA = reward/addiction** (mesolimbic), **substantia nigra = movement/Parkinson's** (nigrostriatal).
- **A-delta vs. C fibers:** fast/sharp "first" pain = A-delta = **wider + myelinated**; slow/dull "second" pain = C = thin + unmyelinated. *Why faster:* myelin enables saltatory conduction and larger diameter lowers axial resistance — both raise conduction velocity.
- **Microglia vs. other glia:** microglia = mesoderm/hematopoietic (immune); astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependymal, and Schwann cells = neuroectoderm.
- **Optic disc (0 cones, blind spot) vs. fovea (max cones, sharpest vision).**

cards.title: Neuromuscular toxins — who relieves spastic paralysis?
cards.body:
**Spastic** (rigid) paralysis = too much muscle contraction. To relieve it, you must **reduce ACh signaling at the neuromuscular junction (which is nicotinic).**

- **Cleaving SNARE proteins (botulinum-style):** blocks ACh *release* → less contraction → **relieves spastic paralysis.** ✓
- **Sarin / organophosphates (AChE inhibitor):** ACh is *not* broken down → **MORE** ACh in the cleft → *worse* spasticity. ✗
- **Atropine (muscarinic blocker):** the NMJ is **nicotinic**, so atropine doesn't act there. ✗

Only SNARE cleavage works. The trap is that all three "sound like" nerve agents — you must track *which receptor* (nicotinic vs. muscarinic) and *which direction* (more vs. less ACh).

cards.title: Action-potential 'all true?' lists are usually FALSE traps
cards.body:
These lists love statements that are subtly wrong; the answer is frequently **None**:
- **Amplitude is all-or-nothing** — a suprathreshold stimulus gives the same-height spike, so amplitude does NOT vary with how fast the cell depolarizes. ✗
- **Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels do NOT stay open longer than K⁺ channels** — Na⁺ channels inactivate quickly; the slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels stay open into the afterhyperpolarization. ✗
- The refractory period is caused by **Na⁺-channel inactivation** (absolute) and **hyperpolarization / K⁺ still open** (relative), not simply "the cell being depolarized following the AP." ✗

Read each clause literally and check the direction. If every statement has a flaw, confidently answer **None** rather than assuming at least one must be true.

cards.title: The odd-one-out senses and reward chemistry
cards.body:
- **The thalamus relays ALL senses to cortex EXCEPT olfaction.** Smell projects straight from the olfactory bulb to olfactory (piriform) cortex, so a total thalamic stroke spares smell but wrecks vision/hearing/touch/taste. Hook: *"smell skips the relay station."*
- **Glutamate** = main excitatory CNS transmitter, mediates **LTP** (learning/memory) via NMDA receptors. **GABA** = its main inhibitory counterpart (Cl⁻).
- **VTA → nucleus accumbens** = mesolimbic **reward/addiction** pathway, dopamine-driven. To treat over-rewarding, you *inhibit* the VTA.

memorize.trigger: Visual pathway from photoreceptor to cortex
memorize.answer: photoreceptor → bipolar → ganglion → optic nerve/tract → LGN (thalamus) → visual cortex
the monoamines — dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine (NOT ACh, glutamate, GABA, glycine)
myopia (nearsighted, eye too long, image in front of retina)

memorize.trigger: Excitatory NT that mediates LTP / learning & memory

memorize.answer: ↑ K⁺ permeability or ↑ extracellular Cl⁻ (NOT ↑ extracellular Na⁺ — Na⁺ permeability is negligible at rest)
all preganglionic (sympathetic + parasympathetic) + all parasympathetic postganglionic; only sympathetic postganglionic uses norepinephrine

memorize.trigger: Caffeine competitively blocks the receptor for

memorize.answer: microglia (brain's immune cells); all other glia are neuroectoderm

memorize.trigger: Region to inhibit to treat dopamine reward/addiction
Increased intraocular pressure / ciliary body overproduces humor / drainage blocked
Retinal cells doing lateral inhibition / edge-sharpening
Sense NOT relayed by the thalamus

memorize.answer: A-delta: wider and myelinated (C fibers = thin, unmyelinated, slow pain); myelin + diameter = faster conduction

practice.note: Ordering question. Start from 'light hits photoreceptors' and follow the signal outward through the retina and back to the brain. Don't be thrown that ganglion cells and optic tract are listed separately — ganglion axons become the optic tract.
practice.solution: Order is bipolar → ganglion → optic tract → LGN, i.e. **3, 2, 4, 1**. Light hits photoreceptors first (given), which synapse onto bipolar cells (3), then ganglion cells (2); ganglion axons form the optic nerve/tract (4), which projects to the LGN of the thalamus (1) before cortex.

practice.note: The permeability-vs-concentration trap. Check each item for what actually moves charge at rest. Only manipulations that add net negative charge inside (or remove positive) hyperpolarize.
practice.solution: **1 and 3.** ↑ K⁺ permeability lets more K⁺ leave (K⁺ equilibrium is very negative) → more negative inside. ↑ extracellular Cl⁻ makes E_Cl more negative and drives Cl⁻ in → negative charge in → more negative. ↑ extracellular Na⁺ (item 2) does almost nothing because resting Na⁺ permeability is negligible — raising a concentration doesn't help if the channel is closed.

practice.note: An 'identify all true' action-potential list — read each clause literally and suspect that all are false. Track Na⁺ vs K⁺ channel timing and the all-or-nothing rule.
practice.solution: **None.** (1) The refractory period is caused by Na⁺-channel inactivation and afterhyperpolarization, not the cell simply being depolarized after the AP. (2) Na⁺ channels inactivate quickly and do NOT stay open longer than K⁺ channels — the slower K⁺ channels stay open into the afterhyperpolarization. (3) AP amplitude is all-or-nothing and does not vary with depolarization speed.

practice.note: The 'neuron 2 vetoes neuron 3' puzzle. Neuron 2 must actively prevent an action potential when co-activated. Ask which option hyperpolarizes / opposes firing on a per-spike basis.
practice.solution: **Z — it increases neuron 3's permeability to Cl⁻.** Opening Cl⁻ channels hyperpolarizes/clamps neuron 3 (an IPSP), canceling neuron 1's excitation. Increasing Na⁺ permeability (Y) would *help* fire it. LTP/LTD (X, W) are slow changes in synaptic strength, not a moment-to-moment veto of a single spike.

practice.note: Autonomic ACh map. Go junction by junction: is it preganglionic, or parasympathetic postganglionic? Only a sympathetic postganglionic synapse would break the pattern.
practice.solution: **ALL.** ACh is the transmitter at every preganglionic autonomic neuron (both parasympathetic and sympathetic) and at all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons. All three listed junctions (parasympathetic pre, parasympathetic post, sympathetic pre) fit — none is a sympathetic *post*ganglionic synapse (the lone norepinephrine exception).

practice.note: Analogy question — ignore the microscopy jargon and extract the mechanism verb: 'deactivate neighbors to sharpen a spot.' Match that to a retinal cell function.
practice.solution: **W — horizontal cells.** STED sharpens by suppressing neighboring fluorophores; that is lateral inhibition, which in the retina is performed by horizontal cells (they inhibit adjacent photoreceptors to enhance contrast/edges). Rods, ganglion, and bipolar cells don't perform this neighbor-suppression role.

subject: bio

why: Evolution is one of the highest-frequency Science Bowl biology subtopics — 14 tracked questions (~4% of the biology bank) — and it's built almost entirely from a small set of recurring conceptual pairs, so a focused lesson converts directly into points.
overview:
## What this topic actually is

Science Bowl "Evolution" is three clusters, and once you own them you own nearly the whole bank:

1. **Selection dynamics + mimicry + coloration** — the big one. Roughly half of all questions are secretly the *same* question: **is this trait fitter when it's COMMON or when it's RARE?** Positive frequency-dependent = common-is-good (aposematic, Müllerian). Negative frequency-dependent = rare-is-good (Batesian, cryptic, self-incompatibility, cichlid sidedness). Watch one trap: *heterozygote advantage* (e.g. sickle-cell/malaria resistance) is balancing selection but **frequency-INDEPENDENT** — it is neither positive nor negative freq-dependent.
2. **Speciation vocabulary** — allo- vs. autopolyploidy, sympatric vs. allopatric, character displacement, punctuated equilibrium, the biological species concept.
3. **Quantitative population genetics** — effective population size, mutation–selection balance, Hardy-Weinberg, and how a new allele's frequency changes over time.

## How it shows up

The signature format is the **"identify all TRUE statements"** bonus and the **"which does NOT..."** tossup. Both are graded on whether you can sort a term into the correct column. There is also a steady drip of one-word recall tossups ("what is this hypothesis?" → punctuated equilibrium; "what is this relationship?" → paralogous) and short ordering/ranking bonuses (rank by effective population size, rank by population change after a predator arrives).

## The smartest way to learn it

Do **not** memorize terms in isolation. Build **two-column tables of the confused pairs** (Batesian vs. Müllerian, ortholog vs. paralog, auto- vs. allopolyploid), and for every row force yourself to state the *mechanism* — why common-is-good, why the bluff needs rarity, why a duplication makes paralogs. The mechanism is what lets you re-derive the answer under buzzer pressure instead of guessing. Memorize the two formulas ($N_e$ and $\hat q$) cold; everything else you should be able to reason out from "safety in numbers" vs. "rare is fair."

cards.title: The master axis: common-is-good vs. rare-is-good
cards.body:
Almost every mimicry/coloration question reduces to one axis:

- **Positive frequency-dependent selection** — a trait gets MORE fit as it gets MORE common. Drives toward fixation. Members: **aposematic (warning) coloration**, **Müllerian mimicry**.
- **Negative frequency-dependent selection** — a trait gets MORE fit as it gets RARER. Maintains a stable polymorphism (equilibrium). Members: **Batesian mimicry**, **cryptic coloration**, **plant self-incompatibility alleles**, **scale-eating cichlid mouth sidedness**.

Do NOT dump **heterozygote advantage** (sickle-cell / malaria resistance) into either bucket: it's *overdominance*, a balancing mechanism that is **frequency-INDEPENDENT** (fitness of the heterozygote doesn't depend on how common the allele is). It maintains polymorphism, but it is neither positive nor negative freq-dependent — a favorite distractor.

When a question lists four traits and asks for the odd one out, this axis is almost always the blade. Aposematic coloration is the classic 'odd one out' in a negative list because it's the one positive item.

cards.title: WHY warning signals are positive (safety in numbers)
cards.body:
A predator only learns to avoid a warning pattern if it **encounters it often** and survives to remember. So the more individuals share the same warning, the faster the whole group gets protected.

- **Aposematic coloration**: each defended prey that shares the pattern reinforces the lesson → the signal is worth more when common.
- **Müllerian mimicry**: two genuinely unpalatable species pool ONE warning pattern, so each predator death educates the predator to avoid BOTH → mutualistic, positive freq-dependent.

Hook: **'safety in numbers — teach the predator once.'** Rarity is death here, because a rare warning never gets learned.

cards.title: WHY bluffs and hiding are negative (rare is fair)
cards.body:
These strategies collapse when they become common:

- **Batesian mimicry** is a **bluff** — a palatable species wears a dangerous species' colors. If bluffers get common, predators keep eating them, learn the pattern is often safe, and stop respecting it. So the bluff only pays while rare.
- **Cryptic coloration** hides from the predator's **search image** (apostatic selection); a rare morph isn't in the predator's expectation set, so it escapes.
- **Self-incompatibility alleles**: a rare S-allele finds more compatible mates (most partners lack it and so won't reject its pollen), so rarity is directly rewarded — this is what maintains dozens of S-alleles.

Hook: **'rare is fair'** — the rare morph wins, which is exactly what keeps the polymorphism balanced.

cards.title: Batesian vs. Müllerian vs. Mertensian
cards.body:
The single most-confused trio:

- **Batesian** = ONE liar. A harmless/**palatable** species mimics a harmful model. Bluff → **negative** freq-dependent. Groups with 'palatable species.'
- **Müllerian** = an HONEST CLUB. Two+ genuinely **unpalatable** species converge on one warning. Mutualistic → **positive** freq-dependent. NOT palatable, NOT a bluff.
- **Mertensian** = the direction is the trap. The **MIMIC is the DEADLY (too-lethal-to-teach) species**; the **MODEL is only MODERATELY venomous** — painful but survivable, so predators live to learn from it. A predator that bites the truly lethal snake dies before it can learn, so lethality can't teach avoidance; the deadly species instead copies the survivable model that actually does the educating.

One-line sort: **Batesian = liar (palatable), Müllerian = honest club (unpalatable), Mertensian = deadly-mimic-of-a-survivable-model.** In a coral-snake triad the harmless kingsnake (Batesian) and the deadly coral snake (Mertensian) both mimic the same moderately-venomous model.

cards.title: Homology family: ortholog / paralog / analogous
cards.body:
**Homologous** genes share common ancestry. Two sub-types:

- **Ortholog** = 'same gene, different species' → diverged by **speciation**.
- **Paralog** = 'copy-paste then diverge, same lineage' → diverged by **gene DUPLICATION**. Lysozyme & α-lactalbumin are the textbook paralogs (one ancestral gene duplicated, drifted to new functions).

Two traps: (1) **analogous** = similar by **convergent evolution**, NOT shared ancestry → it is NEVER a type of homology. (2) When a duplication clue is given, 'homologous' is *technically true* but too vague — the question wants the **most specific** term, **paralogous**. Reflex: hear **'duplicated and diverged'** → answer **paralogous**.

cards.title: Auto- vs. allopolyploidy (and it's sympatric!)
cards.body:
**'Auto = self/one, Allo = other/two.'**

- **Autopolyploidy** = genome doubling WITHIN one species.
- **Allopolyploidy** = two different species hybridize AND the genome doubles. So a 12-chromosome species + a 10-chromosome species → fertile 22-chromosome hybrid is **allopolyploidy** (two genomes combined).

Critical traps on this: polyploid speciation is **sympatric and instant**, NEVER allopatric (no geographic separation needed). It is **common in plants** and arises from **meiotic nondisjunction** errors that double the chromosome set — which is exactly what *restores* fertility to an otherwise-sterile odd-chromosome hybrid (unpaired chromosomes can now pair).

cards.title: Speciation vocabulary you must sort on sight
cards.body:
- **Biological species concept** = reproductively isolated interbreeding populations. Applies ONLY to sexually reproducing organisms → EXCLUDES bacteria (asexual + horizontal gene transfer; e.g. Proteobacteria), INCLUDES mammals (Mammalia) and sexual fungi (e.g. Ascomycota, which reproduce sexually). Rule: **'no sex, no BSC.'**
- **Punctuated equilibrium** (Eldredge & Gould) = long **stasis** broken by rare, rapid change tied to speciation. It's the explicit foil to Darwinian **gradualism**. Buzz phrase: 'significant change restricted to rare, rapid speciation events.'
- **Character displacement** = traits diverge MORE in **sympatry** (overlap) than **allopatry**, because competition selects against similarity. Galápagos finch beaks are the stock example.

cards.title: Effective population size with skewed sex ratio
cards.body:
$$N_e = \dfrac{4 N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}$$

$N_e$ is dragged DOWN toward the **rarer sex** — the limiting sex bottlenecks genetic diversity. For a fixed total, an equal sex ratio maximizes $N_e$.

Worked ranking (rabbits):
- 1M/5F → $N_e = \dfrac{4\cdot1\cdot5}{6} \approx 3.3$
- 3M/3F → $N_e = \dfrac{4\cdot3\cdot3}{6} = 6$
- 12M/2F → $N_e = \dfrac{4\cdot12\cdot2}{14} \approx 6.9$

So increasing order is **1M/5F < 3M/3F < 12M/2F**. Note the wildly skewed 12/2 still beats balanced 3/3 because its raw numbers are much higher — plug the formula, don't eyeball 'balance.'

cards.title: Mutation–selection balance & allele-frequency curves
cards.body:
- **Mutation–selection balance**: a deleterious recessive reaches a STABLE equilibrium $\hat q = \sqrt{\mu/s}$ — mutation keeps injecting it, selection keeps culling it, so it plateaus and is **NEVER fixed**. More mutagens (e.g., **intercalating agents**, which raise $\mu$) push the equilibrium frequency HIGHER. A population sitting at such an equilibrium can still show **Hardy-Weinberg** genotype ratios in any given generation.
- **Beneficial RECESSIVE allele**: rises **slowly then rapidly** to fixation. When rare it hides in heterozygotes, masked from selection ('hidden'); once common, homozygotes appear and selection grips hard ('explosive'). This masking is *Haldane's sieve* — the reason recessive beneficials fix more slowly (and less often) than dominant ones.
- **Beneficial DOMINANT allele**: the mirror image — **fast then slow** (exposed to selection even when rare, then slows as the last copies hide in heterozygotes near fixation).

cards.title: Buzz words → which cluster & what to recall
cards.body:
- 'frequency-dependent,' 'aposematic,' 'cryptic,' 'Batesian/Müllerian/Mertensian,' 'palatable/unpalatable' → **selection + mimicry** cluster; sort on common-vs-rare. ('heterozygote advantage / malaria resistance' → freq-INDEPENDENT overdominance — trap.)
- 'polyploidy,' 'sympatric/allopatric,' 'character displacement,' 'biological species concept,' 'stasis then rapid change' → **speciation** cluster.
- 'effective population size,' 'Hardy-Weinberg,' 'mutation-selection,' 'fixation,' 'reaches equilibrium' → **pop-gen math** cluster.
- 'duplicated and diverged' → **paralogous** (near-reflex; beat the vaguer 'homologous').
- 'restricted to rare rapid speciation' / 'Eldredge and Gould' → **punctuated equilibrium**.
- 'distantly related invertebrates, best DNA marker' → **mitochondrial DNA** (present in all animals — the other candidate markers are absent or lineage-specific).

cards.title: Worked buzz: the coral-snake Mertensian ranking (bank 2025 R13 B22)
cards.body:
Clue: milk snakes are **Batesian** mimics of Sonoran coral snakes; Texas coral snakes are **Mertensian** mimics of Sonoran coral snakes. A non-native predatory falcon is introduced — rank species by *increasing* relative population change. **Answer: 1, 3, 2 (Milk < Texas < Sonoran).**

Step 1 — decode the venom hierarchy from the mimicry types:
- **Milk snake** (Batesian mimic) = harmless / palatable.
- **Texas coral** (Mertensian mimic) = the **DEADLY** one (too lethal to teach on its own).
- **Sonoran coral** (the shared MODEL) = only **moderately venomous** — painful but SURVIVABLE, so it's the snake that actually educates predators.

Step 2 — rank by 'who pays to educate the naive falcon':
- **Sonoran (model) = MOST change**: a falcon that bites it SURVIVES, so that same bird lives on and keeps sampling coral-pattern snakes until it learns — the model absorbs the whole complex's education cost.
- **Texas coral (deadly) = MIDDLE**: a falcon that bites it DIES, removing the predator after a single encounter, so fewer Texas individuals are lost per naive falcon.
- **Milk snake (harmless free-rider) = LEAST change**: it pays nothing to defend or teach and simply rides on the aversion the two venomous species create; once the pattern is feared, it's protected for free.

Mechanism hook: rank by **how much predation each population absorbs before the naive predator stops** — the survivable model pays most, the deadly mimic removes predators fast, the harmless free-rider pays least.

memorize.answer: Batesian mimicry, cryptic coloration, self-incompatibility alleles, scale-eating cichlid mouth sidedness

memorize.trigger: Heterozygote advantage / malaria (sickle-cell) resistance — which freq-dependence?
memorize.answer: NEITHER — it's overdominance, a frequency-INDEPENDENT balancing mechanism (common distractor in freq-dependent questions)
Palatable liar, harmless mimics harmful, negative freq-dependent (only works while rare)
Unpalatable honest club, two+ defended species share a warning, positive freq-dependent, mutualistic

memorize.trigger: Mertensian mimicry — which one is the deadly species, model or mimic?
memorize.answer: The MIMIC is the deadly (too-lethal-to-teach) species; the MODEL is only moderately venomous (survivable, so it teaches predators). A harmless species mimicking that same model = Batesian
Batesian mimicry + cryptic coloration (both undefended: bluff or hide). NOT Müllerian — that requires being genuinely unpalatable
Paralogous (ortholog = speciation; analogous = convergence, not homology; 'homologous' is true but too vague)

memorize.trigger: Two species hybridize + genome doubles → new fertile species
memorize.answer: Allopolyploidy — sympatric, instant, common in plants, from meiotic nondisjunction (doubling restores pairing/fertility)
Only sexual reproducers — excludes bacteria (e.g. Proteobacteria), includes mammals & sexual fungi (Ascomycota)

memorize.trigger: Effective population size, skewed sex ratio formula
memorize.answer: $N_e = 4N_mN_f/(N_m+N_f)$ — dragged toward the rarer sex; equal ratio maximizes it
$\hat q = \sqrt{\mu/s}$ — never fixes; mutagens (intercalators) raise it; a population at it can still satisfy Hardy-Weinberg
Slow first (hidden in heterozygotes — Haldane's sieve), then rapid to fixation; beneficial dominant = fast then slow

memorize.trigger: Eldredge & Gould, change restricted to rare rapid speciation
Best DNA marker for distantly related invertebrates
memorize.answer: Mitochondrial DNA — present in all animals (COI barcoding); beats hemoglobin/lac-repressor/MADS-box, which are absent or lineage-specific

memorize.trigger: Traits more divergent in sympatry than allopatry (finch beaks)

practice.note: 'Positive frequency-dependent' means common-is-good — scan for the item that gets fitter as it spreads. Note the traps: self-incompatibility and cichlid sidedness are negative (rare-is-good) freq-dependent, while malaria resistance is heterozygote advantage (overdominance), which is frequency-INDEPENDENT. None of those three is positive.
practice.solution: Answer: W) Aposematic coloration. Warning coloration is positive freq-dependent because predators only learn to avoid a signal they encounter often — the more individuals share it, the better protected everyone is. Self-incompatibility and cichlid mouth sidedness are negative (rare-favored) freq-dependent; malaria resistance is frequency-independent overdominance. So the only positive-freq-dependent trait is aposematic coloration.

practice.note: Three-part TRUE/FALSE on mimicry. Check each: is Batesian harmless-mimics-harmful? Is Müllerian positive? Is Batesian positive?
practice.solution: Answer: 1 and 2. (1) TRUE — Batesian is a harmless/palatable species mimicking a harmful model. (2) TRUE — Müllerian involves genuinely defended species sharing a warning, so it's positive freq-dependent. (3) FALSE — Batesian is a bluff that only works while rare, so it's NEGATIVE freq-dependent.

practice.note: 'Behaviors found in palatable (undefended) species.' A palatable species has no real defense, so it must either bluff or hide. Which of Müllerian / Batesian / cryptic fits?
practice.solution: Answer: 2 and 3. Batesian mimicry (2) is a palatable bluffer wearing a dangerous model's colors, and cryptic coloration (3) is an undefended species hiding via camouflage — both are strategies of palatable species. Müllerian mimicry (1) requires being genuinely UNpalatable/defended, so it is not a palatable-species behavior.

practice.note: 'Which does NOT exhibit negative freq-dependent selection?' — find the one positive/common-is-good item hiding in a list of rare-is-good traits.
practice.solution: Answer: Z) Aposematic coloration. Self-incompatibility alleles, Batesian mimicry, and cryptic coloration are all negative freq-dependent (favored when rare). Aposematic (warning) coloration is positive freq-dependent — the warning works best when common — so it's the odd one out.

practice.note: Milk snakes are Batesian mimics and Texas coral snakes are Mertensian mimics of Sonoran coral snakes. First decode venom level from the mimicry TYPE (Batesian = harmless; Mertensian mimic = deadly; the shared model = moderately venomous/survivable), then rank by who bears the cost of educating a naive predator.
practice.solution: Answer: 1, 3, 2 (Milk < Texas < Sonoran, increasing change). The Sonoran coral is the moderately-venomous MODEL: a falcon that bites it survives and lives on to keep sampling the pattern, so the model absorbs the most attacks and changes MOST. The Texas coral is the DEADLY Mertensian mimic: it kills the falcon in one encounter, removing the predator quickly, so it changes a moderate amount. The milk snake is the harmless Batesian free-rider — it pays nothing and rides on the aversion the venomous species create, so it changes LEAST.

practice.note: 12-chromosome + 10-chromosome species → fertile 22-chromosome hybrid. Sort each statement. Watch the allopatric trap and the auto- vs. allo- trap.
practice.solution: Answer: 3 and 4. This is ALLOpolyploidy (two species combined), not autopolyploidy, so (2) is false. It's sympatric and instant, not allopatric, so (1) is false. It IS common in plants (3, true) and DOES arise from meiotic nondisjunction that doubles the chromosome set — which restores pairing and fertility to the otherwise-sterile hybrid (4, true).

practice.note: Biological species concept requires interbreeding — 'no sex, no BSC.' Of Proteobacteria, Mammalia, and Ascomycota, which reproduce sexually?
practice.solution: Answer: 2 and 3. Mammalia (mammals) and Ascomycota (sac fungi, which have sexual reproduction) interbreed sexually, so the biological species concept applies. Proteobacteria (1) are asexual prokaryotes with rampant horizontal gene transfer, so the BSC does not apply to them.

practice.note: Diagram of a deleterious recessive allele at mutation-selection balance in three populations. Recall: what does an equilibrium (never fixed) imply, what do mutagens do to the equilibrium frequency, and can such a population still be in Hardy-Weinberg?
practice.solution: Answer: 2 and 3. (1) FALSE — at mutation-selection balance the allele plateaus at q̂=√(μ/s) and NEVER reaches fixation. (2) TRUE — intercalating agents raise the mutation rate μ, which raises the equilibrium frequency, so a population sitting higher could indeed be getting more mutagen exposure. (3) TRUE — a population at mutation-selection equilibrium can still display Hardy-Weinberg genotype ratios in a given generation.

practice.note: Rank by effective population size — do NOT eyeball 'balance,' plug the formula $N_e = 4N_mN_f/(N_m+N_f)$. The rarer sex bottlenecks each population.
practice.solution: Answer: 2, 1, 3. Computing: 1M/5F → 20/6 ≈ 3.3; 3M/3F → 36/6 = 6; 12M/2F → 96/14 ≈ 6.9. Increasing order is 1M/5F (most skewed, lowest) < 3M/3F < 12M/2F. The heavily skewed 12/2 still wins because its raw numbers are large enough to offset the imbalance.

practice.note: A highly beneficial, autosomal-RECESSIVE new allele in a fixed population. Think about where a rare recessive hides and when selection can 'see' it.
practice.solution: Answer: X) slowly at first, then rapidly until fixation. While rare, the recessive allele sits mostly in heterozygotes where it is masked and invisible to selection, so it creeps up slowly (Haldane's sieve). Once common enough that homozygotes appear, the beneficial phenotype is expressed and selection grips hard, driving rapid fixation.

practice.note: Lysozyme and α-lactalbumin: 'an original gene that duplicated and diverged.' Pick the MOST SPECIFIC relationship — don't settle for the vaguer true-but-imprecise option.
practice.solution: Answer: Z) Paralogous. Genes that arise by DUPLICATION within a lineage and then diverge are paralogs. 'Homologous' (Y) is technically true but too vague; 'orthologous' (W) would require divergence by speciation, not duplication; 'analogous' (X) means convergence with no shared ancestry, which is wrong here.

practice.note: 'Most useful DNA source for comparing distantly related INVERTEBRATES.' Eliminate markers that are absent or lineage-specific in invertebrates rather than reaching for a favorite.
practice.solution: Answer: W) Mitochondrial DNA. Every one of these animals has mitochondria, and mtDNA (e.g. COI) is the standard cross-animal comparison marker. Hemoglobin-alpha isn't universal across invertebrates, the lac repressor is a bacterial gene, and the MADS-box is a plant/developmental transcription-factor family — none is broadly useful for invertebrate comparisons.

subject: bio

why: Ecology is ~7% of the Science Bowl biology bank and, unlike biochem, it rewards understanding a handful of models over rote memorization — high point-per-hour once the core pictures click.
overview:
Ecology & Behavior is a **vocabulary-and-model** topic, not a memorize-the-pathway topic. Nearly every question is one of a few recurring themes, and once you know the *model* behind each, the answer falls out. The bank clusters into five areas: **population ecology** (r/K selection, carrying capacity, survivorship curves, dispersion, per-capita growth, Allee effect, the two Lotka-Volterra models), **community ecology** (fundamental vs. realized niche, competitive exclusion, keystone species, island biogeography, interaction signs), **biogeochemical cycles** (nitrogen fixation + eutrophication, phosphorus with no atmospheric step), **ecosystem energetics** (production/trophic efficiency, the 10% rule), and **behavior** (taxis, habituation, mating systems, Bergmann's/Allen's rules).

How it shows up: short-answer buzz terms ("eutrophication," "keystone," "habituation," "polygyny"), quick calculations (per-capita r, production efficiency), and — critically — **"which is NOT true" / "identify all"** formats, which are about a third of the questions. Those formats punish keyword-spotting: you must be able to test *each* option against the model.

The smartest way to learn it: don't flashcard terms in isolation. **Learn the 4-5 core models as pictures** — the logistic/carrying-capacity curve, r vs. K trait lists, Lotka-Volterra predator-prey cross-dependence, competition isoclines, and the three survivorship curves — then hang every vocabulary term on the model it belongs to. Memorize the classic distractor *pairs* cold (semelparous vs. iteroparous, fundamental vs. realized, keystone vs. foundation, taxis vs. kinesis), because those are exactly what the "NOT true" traps exploit.

cards.title: r vs. K selection — the master trait table
cards.body:
Two life-history strategies sit at opposite ends of one axis:

- **r-selected**: many small offspring, little parental care, short life, boom-bust, **semelparous** (one big reproductive event), Type III survivorship, unstable/disturbed habitats. Hook: **r = 'run once.'**
- **K-selected**: few large offspring, high parental care, long life, live near carrying capacity ($K$), density-dependent limits, **iteroparous** (reproduce repeatedly), Type I survivorship. Hook: **K = 'Keep having babies.'**

This single table answers three separate bank questions. The trap is always the same: **semelparous** slipped in as a K-trait — it is r. (Real biology has exceptions like salmon, but Science Bowl uses the clean r=semelparous / K=iteroparous mapping both key on it.)

cards.title: WHY cold-climate animals are big with short limbs (Bergmann + Allen)
cards.body:
This is a surface-area-to-volume argument wearing an ecology costume.

- **Heat loss ∝ surface area**; **heat production ∝ volume (mass).**
- A bigger body has a **smaller SA:V ratio**, so it loses heat slowly relative to how much it makes → poles favor **large bodies (Bergmann's rule).**
- Shorter appendages (ears, limbs, tails) cut surface area further → poles favor **short appendages (Allen's rule).**

Picture the arctic fox (small ears, round) vs. the desert fennec fox (huge ears to *dump* heat). When a question gives you 'heat loss ∝ area, metabolism ∝ volume,' just reason from SA:V — don't recall a fact. Both rules are *within-clade* body-shape trends (Bergmann = size, Allen = appendage length), so keep them paired.

cards.title: WHY nitrogen fixation is the O₂-sensitive step, and how eutrophication cascades
cards.body:
Two separate high-frequency questions, one mechanism each:

- **Fixation** ($N_2 \rightarrow$ ammonia) is run by **nitrogenase, an enzyme irreversibly poisoned by oxygen.** That's WHY fixers hide in anaerobic microenvironments — legume root nodules (leghemoglobin buffers O₂), cyanobacterial heterocysts. Note: *denitrification* is also an anaerobic step, so the true discriminator isn't just 'anaerobic' — it's that fixation's **enzyme is destroyed by O₂**, which makes fixation the classic Science Bowl answer to 'which N-step needs anaerobic conditions.' (Nitrification, by contrast, *requires* O₂.)
- **Eutrophication** is a chain: N/P-rich runoff **fertilizes algae → algal bloom → algae die → decomposers consume O₂ → hypoxic dead zone.** The oxygen crash is caused by *decomposition*, not the algae directly. Buzz phrase 'runoff → bloom → oxygen drops' = eutrophication.

cards.title: WHY each L-V population's equilibrium is set by the OTHER species
cards.body:
The counter-intuitive core of the **Lotka-Volterra predator-prey** model: **the predator equilibrium depends on PREY parameters, and the prey equilibrium depends on PREDATOR parameters** — the rates are cross-wired. From $dx/dt=\alpha x-\beta xy$, $dy/dt=\delta xy-\gamma y$: prey eq. $x^*=\gamma/\delta$ (all predator terms), predator eq. $y^*=\alpha/\beta$ (all prey terms).

Consequences the bank loves:
- Changing rabbit reproduction rate ($\alpha$) does **not** change equilibrium rabbits — it shifts the *fox* equilibrium ($y^*=\alpha/\beta$).
- Changing fox death rate ($\gamma$) shifts the *rabbit* equilibrium ($x^*=\gamma/\delta$).
- Scaling BOTH populations down proportionally (e.g. remove half of each) does **not** move either equilibrium — equilibria are set by rates, not current counts.

So for 'which changes will NOT affect fox equilibrium,' anything that only rescales populations or only touches fox's own death rate leaves fox equilibrium alone; only a change to *rabbit* parameters moves it.

cards.title: Fundamental vs. realized niche + keystone vs. foundation
cards.body:
Two community-ecology distinctions that generate direct questions:

- **Fundamental niche** = the full range a species *could* occupy. **Realized niche** = the smaller range it *actually* occupies after competition/predation. **Realized ≤ fundamental, always.** Pine pushed to the mountaintop by a competitor: whole mountain = fundamental, summit only = realized. This is competitive exclusion in action.
- **Keystone species** = disproportionate impact relative to **low abundance** (sea otters, sea stars). **Foundation/dominant species** = impact from **sheer abundance/biomass** (kelp itself, corals, beavers as ecosystem engineers). Keystone = small number, huge effect; foundation = big number, big effect.

cards.title: Interaction signs, dispersion, and island biogeography
cards.body:
Fast-recall lists:

- **Interaction signs:** mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−, competition −/−. 'At least one organism benefits' → mutualism, commensalism, **and parasitism** (the parasite benefits!). Only competition has no beneficiary.
- **Dispersion:** clumped (most common — patchy resources or social grouping, e.g. starfish in tide pools), uniform (territorial/allelopathy — active spacing), random (rare, requires no interaction and uniform resources).
- **Island biogeography (MacArthur-Wilson):** richness rises with island **size** (bigger = more habitat, lower extinction) and **proximity to mainland** (closer = higher immigration). Max diversity = **large + near**; equilibrium is a *dynamic* balance where immigration rate = extinction rate (species turnover continues).

cards.title: Buzz words → answer reflexes
cards.body:
The word tells you the answer:
- 'reproduces once / single reproductive event' → **semelparous** (r). 'reproduces repeatedly' → **iteroparous** (K).
- 'runoff → algal bloom → oxygen drops' → **eutrophication**. 'which N-step needs anaerobic conditions / is inhibited by O₂' → **nitrogen fixation** (nitrogenase).
- 'no atmospheric reservoir' → **phosphorus cycle.**
- 'disproportionate impact / sea otters / small numbers, big effect' → **keystone species.**
- 'directed movement toward/away from a stimulus / moth to light' → **taxis** (vs. undirected **kinesis**).
- 'stops responding to a repeated harmless stimulus' → **habituation.**
- 'ornamented males, one male many females' → **polygyny.**
- 'cold-climate body shape' → **Bergmann (larger body) + Allen (shorter appendages).**
- 'Mediterranean, fire-adapted shrubs, dry summers' → **chaparral.**

cards.title: Worked buzz: the bear production-efficiency calc
cards.body:
Clue: 'Bear ingests 400 kJ; 150 kJ egested as waste; 120 kJ to respiration; 130 kJ to new biomass. Production efficiency?'

**Production efficiency = new biomass ÷ ASSIMILATED energy** (not ÷ ingested — that's the trap).
- Assimilated = ingested − egested = $400 - 150 = 250$ kJ.
- Efficiency = $130 / 250 = 0.52 = $ **52%**.

The respiration number (120) is a distractor — it's already inside assimilated (250 = 120 respiration + 130 biomass). The single decision that makes or breaks this: **divide by assimilated, not by the 400 you ate.** (The ~10% rule is a *different* quantity — trophic-level transfer efficiency between organisms, not within one.)

cards.title: Worked buzz: per-capita rate of increase r
cards.body:
Clue: 'Wolves grow 16 → 28 → 49 with abundant resources. Annual per-capita rate of increase?'

**During exponential growth, $r = (N_{t+1} - N_t)/N_t$.**
- Year 1: $(28-16)/16 = 12/16 = 0.75.$
- Check year 2: $(49-28)/28 = 21/28 = 0.75.$ Constant → confirms exponential.

Answer: **0.75 (75%).** The check step matters: exponential growth means a *constant* per-capita rate, so computing both intervals both verifies your arithmetic and confirms the model applies (equivalently, $N_{t+1}=N_t(1+r)$ with a fixed multiplier 1.75).

cards.title: The distractor pairs that sink students
cards.body:
Memorize the *difference*, cold — these are what 'NOT true'/'identify all' items exploit:
- **Semelparous vs. iteroparous** — #1 trap. K = iteroparous; the 'NOT a K-trait' answer is *always* semelparous.
- **Fundamental vs. realized niche** — realized is the SMALLER, post-competition one.
- **Keystone vs. foundation** — keystone = low abundance/high impact; foundation = high abundance/biomass drives impact.
- **Taxis vs. kinesis** — taxis is *directed* (toward/away); kinesis is *undirected* (random speed/turning change).
- **Assimilated vs. ingested** in efficiency math — divide by assimilated (ingested − feces).
- **Allee causes vs. non-causes** — mate-finding/cooperation/colonies/group defense cause it (being RARE hurts); **faster disease spread at high density does NOT** (crowding *worsens* disease, the opposite direction).
- **Type II survivorship** — constant *per-capita* mortality rate; a straight line only on a **log (semi-log)** axis, never on raw counts.

cards.title: 'A population can never exceed its carrying capacity' is FALSE
cards.body:
Carrying capacity ($K$) is a long-run equilibrium, not a hard ceiling. Populations routinely **overshoot** $K$ (lag in density-dependent feedback), then crash back down or oscillate around it. So 'a population can never exceed $K$' is a classic **NOT-true** answer.

What *is* true about $K$: per-capita growth rate decreases as $N \to K$ (and is 0 at $N=K$); abiotic factors can lower $K$; habitat corridors/added resources can raise $K$. Also remember $K$ is not fixed — it shifts with resources and conditions. When a carrying-capacity 'which is NOT true' appears, the overshoot statement is your prime suspect.

memorize.answer: Iteroparous (reproduce repeatedly); semelparous is r-selected — the #1 trap answer

memorize.trigger: Which N-cycle step needs anaerobic conditions / is inhibited by O₂
memorize.answer: Nitrogen fixation (its enzyme nitrogenase is destroyed by O₂; note denitrification is also anaerobic, but fixation is the intended answer)
Eutrophication (O₂ crash is from decomposers, not the algae directly)

memorize.trigger: Biogeochemical cycle with no atmospheric reservoir

memorize.answer: New biomass ÷ assimilated energy, where assimilated = ingested − egested (feces)
(N_t+1 − N_t) / N_t during exponential growth (constant each interval)

memorize.trigger: Lotka-Volterra: what sets each population's equilibrium
memorize.answer: The OTHER species' parameters — prey eq. x*=γ/δ (predator rates), predator eq. y*=α/β (prey rates)

memorize.trigger: Interaction signs: mutualism / commensalism / parasitism / competition

memorize.answer: Large island close to the mainland (big = low extinction, near = high immigration)

memorize.trigger: Moth orienting to a light source (directed movement)
Animal stops responding to a repeated harmless stimulus
Ornamented males, one male mates with many females

memorize.answer: Larger body (Bergmann) + shorter appendages (Allen) — lower SA:V retains heat

memorize.trigger: Sea otters in kelp forest / low abundance, huge effect
memorize.answer: Keystone species (vs. foundation = impact from high abundance/biomass)

practice.note: K-selection trait recall in a 'NOT characteristic' frame — the highest-frequency trap in the whole topic. Test each option against the r/K table rather than pattern-matching.
practice.solution: Answer: W) Semelparous. K-selected species live near carrying capacity (Z), face density-dependent limits (X), and show Type I survivorship (Y) — all three are true K-traits. Semelparity (one big reproductive event) is an r-strategy; K-selected species are iteroparous, reproducing repeatedly over a long life. This exact trap recurs across years (see, where semelparous is again the odd-one-out among K-traits).

practice.note: The calculation hinges on ONE decision: divide by assimilated, not by ingested. The respiration number is a distractor already contained in the assimilated total.
practice.solution: Answer: 52%. Production efficiency = new biomass ÷ assimilated energy. Assimilated = ingested − egested = 400 − 150 = 250 kJ. Efficiency = 130 / 250 = 0.52 = 52%. Dividing by the ingested 400 (giving 32.5%) is the classic error; the 120 kJ of respiration is a decoy since assimilated = 120 (respiration) + 130 (biomass).

practice.note: An 'identify all that will NOT affect' Lotka-Volterra item — you must apply the cross-dependence rule to each option, not spot a keyword. (Option 1's stem says 'wolves' but means the foxes — a typo; treat predator = fox throughout.)
practice.solution: Answer: 1 and 3. In L-V predator-prey dynamics the fox (predator) equilibrium is y*=α/β, set entirely by the PREY's parameters. (1) Removing half of each population only rescales counts, not rates → equilibria unchanged. (3) Decreasing fox life expectancy raises the predator death rate γ, which shifts the PREY equilibrium x*=γ/δ, not the fox's own → fox equilibrium unchanged. Only (2), increasing rabbit reproduction (α), changes a prey parameter and therefore DOES move the fox equilibrium y*=α/β — so it's excluded.

practice.note: Allee-effect causes: keep the logic 'why does being RARE hurt?' The disease option is the reliable distractor because crowding worsens disease, which is the opposite direction.
practice.solution: Answer: 1 and 2. The Allee effect means per-capita growth slows at SMALL population sizes — so valid causes are things that require a crowd. (1) Reciprocal altruism and (2) living in colonies both need numbers to work, so being rare hurts → valid Allee causes. (3) Transmissible disease spreads FASTER at high density, so a large population is disadvantaged by it — that's the reverse of an Allee cause, so it's excluded (mirrors, where 'disease spreads more rapidly at small sizes' is the NOT-valid explanation).

practice.note: Pure recall, but reason from mechanism: which nutrient has no common gaseous form? Water, carbon, and nitrogen all cycle through the atmosphere.
practice.solution: Answer: Z) Phosphorus cycle. Phosphorus has no significant gaseous phase, so it moves only through rock, soil, water, and organisms (weathering → uptake → sedimentation). Carbon (CO₂), nitrogen (N₂), and water (vapor) all use the atmosphere as a major reservoir. Memory hook: 'P for Pavement/rock, not air.'

practice.note: A 'NOT true' survivorship item. The trap is the word 'linear' — Type II is a straight line only on a LOG axis, and you must also know which taxa fit Type II vs. Type III.
practice.solution: Answer: Y) A molting crab species would follow a linear type II survivorship curve. Type II means a constant per-capita mortality rate across life (W true), which plots as a straight line on a semi-log axis — not on a raw-count axis. Songbirds are a standard Type II example (X true), and Type II species have lower early mortality than Type III species (Z true). Molting crabs (and most invertebrates) suffer heavy larval/early mortality with survivors persisting — that's Type III, not a 'linear Type II,' so the statement is false.

subject: bio

why: Worth ~6.6% of the bio bank (23 questions), and it is unusually learnable: two frameworks — the endosymbiosis family tree and the Gram-stain mechanism — plus a short list of repeat-offender facts cover almost all of it. The payoff per hour is high because the same clues recur nearly verbatim across years.
overview:
This is the **"small living things"** cluster: bacteria, archaea, viruses/viroids, protists, and a bit of fungi. In the Science Bowl bank it's dominated by a handful of repeat offenders — **Gram staining, protist endosymbiosis lineages, dinoflagellate closed mitosis, malaria, and HIV/retroviruses** — so learning ~10 concepts cold covers most of the 23 questions.

**How it shows up.** Roughly a third are straight recall ("what appendage in conjugation?" → pilus). Another third are **NOT / EXCEPT** questions that invert the answer (which feature is *not* shared by archaea and bacteria? which HIV part is *not* genome-encoded?). The last third are **ordering / ranking** problems — Gram reagent sequence, Winogradsky column depth, relatedness of algal clades. Those ranking questions are where people whiff, because they need a *mechanism*, not a flashcard.

**Smartest way to learn it.** Don't memorize protists as a list of weird names. Learn two frameworks and everything else falls out:
- The **endosymbiosis family tree** — who engulfed a *green* alga (euglenids) vs. a *red* alga (alveolates + stramenopiles: apicomplexans, dinoflagellates, diatoms, brown algae).
- The **Gram-stain mechanism** — thick vs. thin peptidoglycan wall → whether the crystal-violet complex survives the alcohol wash.
