Those two alone answer at least 8 questions and turn "ranking" traps into logic instead of guessing. Everything else is a small pile of vocabulary gimmes (zoonotic, thermophile, quorum sensing) you drill to reflex.

cards.title: Gram stain reads the cell WALL, not the membrane
cards.body:
Gram staining sorts bacteria by **cell-wall** structure, and the answer is *always* the wall — "cell membrane" is an explicit **DO NOT ACCEPT**.

- **Gram-positive** = thick peptidoglycan → traps dye → stains **purple**.
- **Gram-negative** = thin wall + outer membrane → dye washes out → counterstains **pink**.

Reagent order (mnemonic **"Come In And Stain"**):
**C**rystal violet → **I**odine (mordant) → **A**lcohol (decolorize) → **S**afranin (counterstain).

cards.title: WHY the crystal violet stays (or leaves)
cards.body:
The mechanism is physical trapping, not chemistry you memorize. Iodine (the *mordant*) locks crystal violet into a big **CV–iodine complex** inside the peptidoglycan mesh.

- **Thick wall (Gram+):** alcohol *dehydrates and shrinks* the dense mesh, closing its pores so the complex can't escape → stays purple.
- **Thin wall (Gram−):** alcohol dissolves the lipid outer membrane, and the thin mesh can't retain the complex → washes out → safranin then dyes it pink.

Corollary the bank loves: if a **Gram− sample looks purple**, the usual cause is **too many cell layers** smeared on the slide — alcohol physically can't reach the deeper cells to decolorize them. It's the same trapping logic in reverse.

cards.title: The endosymbiosis family tree (green vs. red)
cards.body:
One tree answers 3+ questions. A eukaryote ate a photosynthetic alga; *which* alga marks the lineage.

- **Green alga engulfed → Euglenids** (and chlorarachniophytes).
- **Red alga engulfed → Alveolates + Stramenopiles**: **Apicomplexans (Plasmodium/malaria)**, **Dinoflagellates (red tide)**, **Diatoms**, and **brown algae**.

WHY it's testable as logic: all the classic "marine photosynthesizer" protists (diatoms, dinos, brown algae) trace to the **RED** line, so ranking them by relatedness is just reading the tree. Two traps: (1) **Apicomplexans (malaria) are on the RED line even though they aren't photosynthetic** — their apicoplast is a leftover red-alga plastid. (2) **Trypanosoma** (African sleeping sickness) is a euglenozoan — same broad group as the green-line euglenids but non-photosynthetic — and is **NOT** a red-alga engulfer, the classic bait in "identify all" questions.

cards.title: Viruses, retroviruses, viroids, prions — the ladder
cards.body:
Order of increasing structure:
- **Prion** = misfolded **protein only**, no nucleic acid.
- **Viroid** = naked **RNA only**, no protein, no capsid.
- **Virus** = nucleic acid (RNA *or* DNA) **+ protein capsid**, sometimes an envelope.

**HIV** = **retrovirus**, single-stranded **RNA** genome, uses **reverse transcriptase** (RNA → DNA). Its lipid **envelope is stolen from the host membrane** as the virus buds out — only the envelope *proteins/spikes* are viral, so the lipid envelope itself is **NOT genome-encoded**. **Coronaviridae** (SARS/COVID) are also **ssRNA** (but not retroviruses — no reverse transcriptase).

cards.title: Buzz words → reflex answer
cards.body:
- "differentiates bacteria by **structure**" / "crystal violet" / "safranin" → **Gram stain (cell WALL)**
- "**cytoplasmic channels/tunnels through an intact nucleus** during mitosis" → **dinoflagellate (closed mitosis)**
- "**sole vector Anopheles**" / "protist-borne disease" / "apical complex" → **Plasmodium / Apicomplexa / malaria**
- "**reverse transcriptase**" / "retrovirus" → **HIV, single-stranded RNA**
- "**glass-like / silica / $SiO_2$** cell wall, makes oxygen" → **diatoms**
- "hairlike appendage, conjugation, **retracts**" → **pilus**
- "jumps from **animals to humans**" → **zoonotic**
- "survives **high temp / hydrothermal vents / black smokers**" → **thermophiles**
- "regulates **biofilm by population density**" → **quorum sensing**
- "**naked RNA, no protein** / lowest sulfur signal" → **viroid**
- "anaerobic **reduced mitochondria** in a protist" → **hydrogenosome (Trichomonas)**

cards.title: Worked buzz: the disguised malaria clue
cards.body:
**Clue:** *"Identify all that underwent secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga: 1) causative agent of African sleeping sickness; 2) organism for which the Anopheles mosquito is the sole vector; 3) organisms that cause red tide."*

**How to land it fast:**
1. Decode the riddles: (1) = **Trypanosoma** (a euglenozoan), (2) = **Plasmodium** (malaria, an apicomplexan), (3) = **dinoflagellates** (red tide, alveolates).
2. Apply the tree: euglenozoans sit on the green side of the split; the red-alga line is **alveolates + stramenopiles** (apicomplexans + dinoflagellates).
3. So **2 and 3** are red-alga engulfers; 1 (Trypanosoma) is not. **Answer: 2 and 3.**

The whole question is the endosymbiosis tree wearing a disguise. Anopheles/red-tide phrasing is how they point at Plasmodium and dinoflagellates without naming them.

cards.title: Ordering problems: Gram sequence & Winogradsky depth
cards.body:
Two ranking questions recur — both are mechanism, not memory.

**Gram reagent order:** Crystal violet → Iodine → Alcohol → Safranin. (If they say "not decolorizing with ethanol," the remaining order is still CV → iodine → safranin, i.e. **2, 3, 1** for that stem.)

**Winogradsky column, top → bottom = decreasing oxygen:**
- **Top (aerobic + light):** cyanobacteria
- **Middle (facultative):** yeast
- **Bottom (strict anaerobe):** *C. difficile*

It's an oxygen/light gradient in mud. Order anything by **oxygen tolerance high→low** and you can't miss it.

cards.title: Archaea vs. Bacteria — histones are the split
cards.body:
Both are prokaryotes: **no nucleus, single circular chromosome, no membrane-bound organelles, ribosomes** — all shared.

The **NOT-shared** feature the bank uses: **archaea package their DNA with HISTONES; bacteria do NOT.** Archaea's information machinery (histones, RNA polymerase, transcription factors, translation) is the eukaryote-like part — *that's* why the frame **"archaea sit closer to us (eukaryotes) than bacteria do"** works. (Careful: archaeal **membrane lipids are the opposite of eukaryote-like** — they're ether-linked branched isoprenoids **unique to archaea**, while bacteria and eukaryotes both use ester-linked fatty acids; archaea also lack true peptidoglycan.) So on "which is NOT a shared feature?", the answer is **lack of histones** — because archaea don't lack them.

cards.title: The classic distractor pairs — memorize the split
cards.body:
- **Cell WALL vs. cell membrane** — Gram stain is always the wall; membrane is a DO-NOT-ACCEPT.
- **Green vs. red endosymbiosis** — euglenids = GREEN; Plasmodium, dinoflagellates, diatoms, brown algae = RED (Plasmodium is red-line despite being non-photosynthetic).
- **Archaea vs. bacteria** — archaea HAVE histones; "lack of histones" is bacteria-only.
- **Envelope proteins (viral) vs. envelope lipid (host)** — HIV encodes the spikes, NOT the lipid envelope.
- **Viroid (RNA only) vs. virus (nucleic acid + capsid) vs. prion (protein only)** — sulfur signal: prion high, viroid **lowest**.
- **Pilus (conjugation/attachment) vs. flagellum (motility).**
- **Karyogamy BEFORE meiosis** in fungi — "meiosis precedes karyogamy" is FALSE; the order is reversed.

cards.title: WHY viroids give the lowest sulfur signal
cards.body:
Trick question tell: a stain that binds **sulfur** is really detecting **protein**, because sulfur lives in the amino acids **cysteine and methionine**.

- **Prion** = pure protein → high sulfur.
- **Bacteria / virus** = have proteins → sulfur present.
- **Viroid** = a bare RNA circle, **no protein at all** → essentially **no sulfur → lowest fluorescence**.

Same reasoning powers any "which has the least protein?" framing: viroid wins because it's the only protein-free pathogen on the list. (Nucleic acids contain no sulfur — the S is a protein marker.)

cards.title: NOT / EXCEPT framing flips over half these questions
cards.body:
More than half of this topic's questions are worded to **invert** the answer. Read the stem twice and mark the polarity before choosing.

Common inversions:
- "Which is **NOT** encoded by the HIV genome?" → the **envelope (lipid)**.
- "Which is **NOT** a shared feature of archaea and bacteria?" → **lack of histones**.
- "Which statement about basidiomycetes is **NOT** true?" → "**meiosis precedes karyogamy**" (it's the reverse).

In fungi, cytoplasm fuses first (**plasmogamy**), a long **dikaryotic** stage follows, then nuclei fuse (**karyogamy**), and only then **meiosis**. So any "meiosis first" claim is the false one.

memorize.answer: Cell WALL structure (thick vs. thin peptidoglycan) — NOT the membrane
Crystal violet → Iodine (mordant) → Alcohol (decolorize) → Safranin ('Come In And Stain')
Gram+ = purple (thick peptidoglycan); Gram− = pink (thin wall + outer membrane)
Alveolates + stramenopiles: apicomplexans (malaria), dinoflagellates (red tide), diatoms, brown algae
Apicomplexa / Plasmodium / Anopheles mosquito (protist-borne, not bacterial or viral)

memorize.trigger: Cytoplasmic channels through an intact nucleus during mitosis
HIV part NOT encoded by the genome
memorize.answer: The lipid envelope (host-derived; only the spike proteins are viral)
Viroid (naked RNA, no protein at all)

memorize.trigger: NOT shared by archaea and bacteria
memorize.answer: Lack of histones — archaea HAVE histones, bacteria don't
Ether-linked branched isoprenoids — UNIQUE to archaea (bacteria & eukaryotes use ester-linked fatty acids)
Cyanobacteria → yeast → C. difficile (oxygen high → low)

memorize.trigger: Silica / $SiO_2$ glass cell wall, big O2 producer
Anaerobic reduced mitochondria in a protist
Bacteria coordinate biofilm by population density
Pathogen that jumps from animals to humans

memorize.answer: Plasmogamy → dikaryotic stage → karyogamy (nuclear fusion) → meiosis; 'meiosis first' is false

practice.note: An 'identify all' endosymbiosis question in disguise — every organism is given as a riddle, not a name. Decode each before applying the tree, and don't get baited by the sleeping-sickness organism.
practice.solution: Decode: (1) African sleeping sickness = Trypanosoma, a euglenozoan (green side of the split, non-photosynthetic — never underwent red-alga endosymbiosis); (2) Anopheles' sole-vector organism = Plasmodium, an apicomplexan (RED line); (3) red tide = dinoflagellates, alveolates (RED line). Red-alga secondary endosymbiosis produced alveolates + stramenopiles, so Plasmodium and dinoflagellates qualify but Trypanosoma does not. Answer: 2 and 3.

practice.note: Ordering by column depth. Don't memorize three names — reason from the oxygen/light gradient in the mud (top = oxygen-rich and lit, bottom = anoxic).
practice.solution: Winogradsky columns stratify by oxygen tolerance. Top: photosynthetic aerobes = cyanobacteria (2). Middle: facultative anaerobe = yeast (3). Bottom: strict anaerobe = C. difficile (1). Top→bottom = 2, 3, 1.

practice.note: A relatedness ranking that's pure tree-reading. Brown algae are stramenopiles on the RED-alga line; ask how close each clade sits to that node.
practice.solution: Increasing relatedness to brown algae: red algae are the most distant (they're the engulfed ancestor, outside the crown group) → dinoflagellates are alveolates (sister group within the SAR/red lineage) → diatoms are stramenopiles, the SAME group as brown algae, so closest. Order = 2 (red algae), 3 (dinoflagellates), 1 (diatoms).

practice.note: A NOT question about viral anatomy. Reverse transcriptase, capsid, and glycoproteins are all proteins the virus builds; think about where the membrane comes from.
practice.solution: An enveloped virus buds through the host cell and wraps itself in host membrane, so the lipid ENVELOPE is host-derived and not encoded by the viral genome — only the envelope glycoproteins (spikes), capsid, and reverse transcriptase are genome-encoded. Answer: Y) viral envelope.

practice.note: The 'sulfur' label is a stand-in for 'protein.' Rank the pathogen classes by how much protein each contains.
practice.solution: Sulfur occurs in cysteine and methionine (not in nucleic acids), so a sulfur-binding stain reports protein content. Prions are pure protein (high), bacteria and viruses contain proteins (present), but viroids are naked RNA circles with no protein at all — essentially no sulfur, hence the lowest fluorescence. Answer: Y) viroid.

practice.note: A mechanism question dressed as lab troubleshooting. E. coli is Gram-negative, so it SHOULD end up pink; explain why it wrongly reads purple.
practice.solution: Gram-negatives decolorize because alcohol flushes the crystal violet–iodine complex through their thin wall. If too many cells are smeared in overlapping layers, alcohol physically can't reach and decolorize the deeper cells, so they retain the purple dye and the sample looks falsely Gram-positive. Answer: X) they smeared too many cell layers on the slide.

subject: bio

why: ~7.5% of the bio bank and one of the most calculation-heavy topics — mastering a handful of formulas (multiplication rule, Hardy-Weinberg, recombination) lets you brute-force half the questions, and the recognition rules (inheritance patterns, mutation types, disorders) are pure high-yield recall.
overview:
## What this topic covers

Genetics & Heredity is **~80% math, 20% vocabulary**. Almost every question is one of two shapes:

- **"Compute the number/fraction"** — cross two heterozygotes, apply Hardy-Weinberg, work a linkage problem, count Barr bodies or chromosomes. These reward a *tiny* set of reusable formulas, not memorization.
- **"Which pattern/term"** — recognize X-linked vs. mitochondrial vs. Z-linked from a verbal clue, name a mutation type, or match a disorder to its enzyme (albinism → tyrosinase).

## How it shows up in Science Bowl

The bank leans hard on **probability arithmetic you can do in your head** if you know the multiplication rule. A trihybrid cross, a Hardy-Weinberg prevalence, a lethal-recessive survivor count — each is a 15-second plug-and-chug once you spot the trigger word. The recognition tossups (mitochondrial "passes to all her children," "worsens each generation" = triplet repeat) are fast points if you drilled the tells.

## The smartest way to learn it

**Do not flashcard the questions.** Learn ~6 formulas and ~5 pattern rules *cold* and every question becomes plug-and-play. In priority order:

1. **Multiplication rule** — break any multi-gene cross into independent single-gene probabilities and multiply. This alone cracks the most questions.
2. **Hardy-Weinberg** — recessive phenotype $= q^2$, so square-root first; carriers $= 2pq$ (never $q$).
3. **Recombination frequency** — 50% unlinked, 0% fully linked.
4. Then layer on the **inheritance-pattern tells**, **mutation types**, and **chromosome-disorder facts** — all pure recognition.

Every fact below comes with its *why* so it sticks as a mechanism, not a memorized string.

cards.title: The $3^n$ / $2^n$ multiplication rule (the master key)
cards.body:
For a self-cross of an **$n$-way heterozygote** (assuming **complete dominance** and **independent assortment**):

- **$3^n$ genotypes**, **$2^n$ phenotypes**.
- For *any specific* combination, multiply the single-gene probabilities.

**Single locus $Aa \times Aa$** gives 1 AA: 2 Aa: 1 aa → 3/4 dominant, 1/4 recessive, and P(homozygous) = 1/2, P(het) = 1/2.

Because genes assort independently, you **multiply**:
- 4-way het cross → $3^4 = 81$ genotypes.
- Trihybrid, P(all three dominant) = $(3/4)^3 = 27/64$.

**Why it works:** each locus is an independent event, so the counting rule for independent events (multiply) applies. This single rule is the highest-frequency skill in the entire topic.

cards.title: WHY carriers = $2pq$ and you must square-root first
cards.body:
Hardy-Weinberg: $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$, with $p+q=1$.

The **gateway move is always the same**: a recessive *disease/phenotype* frequency **IS** $q^2$ (only homozygous-recessive individuals show the trait). So:

1. Take the given prevalence = $q^2$.
2. **Square-root it** to get $q$.
3. $p = 1-q$.
4. Carriers (heterozygotes) $= 2pq$.

Example: prevalence $1/400 \Rightarrow q = 1/20$, $p = 19/20$, carriers $= 2(19/20)(1/20) = 19/200$.

**Why the trap works:** students report $q$ (the allele frequency) when asked for *carriers*. A carrier is one **person** built from **two** alleles — one rare, one common — which is exactly the $2pq$ middle term. When the disease is rare ($p\approx1$), $2pq \approx 2q$, so carriers are roughly **double** the rare-allele frequency and vastly outnumber affected individuals. Recall: 'carrier = het = the $2pq$ term.'

cards.title: WHY recombination frequency maxes out at 50%
cards.body:
**Independent assortment produces exactly 50% recombinants** — that's the ceiling. So RF can never exceed 50%.

- **RF = 50%** → genes on *different* chromosomes (or so far apart they behave that way).
- **RF = 0%** → *completely linked* genes → only parental gametes exist.
- **$1\%$ RF = 1 map unit (centimorgan).**

Gamete math for RF = 20%: recombinants total 20% (10% + 10%), parentals total 80% (40% + 40%). General rule: **recombinant gametes split RF/2 each; parental gametes split $(1-\text{RF})/2$ each.**

**Mechanism hook:** crossing over between two loci swaps their alleles onto the homolog. Closer loci = fewer crossovers between them = fewer recombinants = lower RF. Fully linked → a parent carrying *wrinkled+yellow* on one homolog throws **only** wrinkled-yellow and smooth-green gametes; the two 'new' combos (wrinkled-green, smooth-yellow) have $P=0$ because no crossover ever separates the linked alleles.

cards.title: Inheritance-pattern tells (recognition scripts)
cards.body:
Match the verbal clue to the pattern:

- **Mitochondrial** — mother → **ALL** her children; fathers transmit to none (sperm mitochondria are excluded from the egg). ('Mom passes to all 6 kids; her brother passes to none of his 54.')
- **Y-linked** — father → **all sons only**, never daughters.
- **X-linked recessive** — skips generations, mostly males, **no male-to-male transmission** (dad gives sons his Y, not his X).
- **Autosomal dominant** — every affected child has an affected parent; no skipping.
- **Autosomal recessive** — can skip generations, both sexes equally.

**Fast elimination:** a father-to-son transmission clue instantly rules OUT everything X-linked and mitochondrial. 'Lowest chance a daughter is affected when only the mother is affected' → **X-linked recessive**: an unaffected father must carry a healthy X (or he'd be affected), and he gives that guaranteed-healthy X to every daughter, so she can never inherit the two bad alleles she'd need. (Autosomal recessive can't guarantee 0 — the unaffected father might be a silent carrier.)

cards.title: Z-linked is X-linked with the sexes flipped
cards.body:
In **birds, butterflies, and many reptiles/snakes**: males are **ZZ**, females are **ZW**. The **female is the hemizygous (heterogametic) sex** — she's the 'human male' of sex-linked genetics.

- A Z-linked **recessive** trait shows up in a female ($Z^a W$) with a **single** allele.
- Daughter (ZW) of an **affected male** ($Z^a Z^a$) always gets his $Z^a$ (her W comes from mom) → she is $Z^a W$ → **100% affected**.
- Hardy-Weinberg for Z-linked: female phenotype frequency = $q$ directly (she has one Z), so 'affected females' gives you $q$ **without square-rooting**.

**Rule:** take every 'affected males' argument from mammals and swap it to 'affected females' for birds.

cards.title: Chromosome counting: Barr bodies, nondisjunction, relatedness
cards.body:
**Barr bodies $= (\#X) - 1$** per cell (all X's but one are inactivated for dosage compensation; Y's don't count).
- XX → 1; XY → 0; XXXYY → $3-1 = 2$.

**Nondisjunction:** failure to separate.
- Meiosis **I** failure = homologs don't separate → **all 4** gametes abnormal.
- Meiosis **II** failure = sister chromatids don't separate → only **2 of 4** gametes abnormal (affects **fewer**).
- Trisomy = 47, Monosomy = 45.

**Coefficient of relatedness $r$** (halve at each meiotic step):
- Parent–offspring, full sibs = **1/2**
- Grandparent, half-sib, aunt/uncle = **1/4**
- First cousins = **1/8**
- **Inbreeding raises these** — because the two parents also share genes, a child of full-sibling parents shares $\approx$**0.75** with a parent (using $r = 2\times$ kinship).

cards.title: Buzz words → what to grab
cards.body:
- **'heterozygous for N traits,' 'dihybrid/trihybrid,' 'self-cross F1'** → $3^n$/$2^n$, multiply single-gene odds.
- **'Hardy-Weinberg,' 'prevalence,' 'carrier frequency,' '% affected'** → $q^2$ = recessive %, **square-root first**; carriers = $2pq$.
- **'recombination frequency,' 'map units,' 'linked,' 'crossing over'** → RF (50% unlinked, 0% fully linked).
- **'passes to all her children / none of his'** → mitochondrial (maternal); **'father → only sons'** → Y-linked.
- **'gets worse each generation,' 'anticipation'** → trinucleotide repeat expansion.
- **'karyotype,' 'nondisjunction,' 'trisomy,' 'Barr body'** → chromosome counting.
- **'seedless,' 'weak seeds,' 'pairing problems in meiosis'** → odd polyploid (triploid).
- **'tyrosinase,' 'no melanin'** → albinism.
- **'true-breeding × true-breeding → intermediate'** → incomplete dominance (het is a countable phenotype).

cards.title: Worked buzz: '16% black chickens → % blue?'
cards.body:
**Clue:** black × white true-breeders give **blue** offspring (incomplete dominance → heterozygote is visibly intermediate; this is the Andalusian fowl). In HW equilibrium, 16% are black. Find blue %.

**Land it:**
1. Black = homozygous → $q^2 = 0.16$.
2. Square-root: $q = 0.4$, so $p = 0.6$.
3. Blue = heterozygotes = $2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48$ → **48%**.

**Why it's fast:** the phrase 'true-breeding × true-breeding → intermediate' flags **incomplete dominance**, which makes the heterozygote class ($2pq$) a directly *countable* phenotype (blue). Same HW machinery — but now the $2pq$ middle term is a visible phenotype rather than an invisible carrier count.

cards.title: Worked buzz: lethal recessive → conditioning on survival
cards.body:
**Clue:** two carriers ($Aa \times Aa$) have 120 children; the disease kills $aa$ before birth. How many *survivors* are carriers?

**Land it:**
1. Punnett: 1 AA: 2 Aa: 1 aa.
2. The **aa die** before birth → they were never counted among the 120. Renormalize over the surviving **3** classes: 1 AA: 2 Aa.
3. Carriers = **2/3** of survivors → $120 \times 2/3 = $ **80**.

**Why the trick lives here:** because $aa$ die *before birth*, the 120 'children' are already the survivors, so the $aa$ quarter is gone. Conditioning on survival turns the 1:2:1 into 1:2, and 'what fraction are carriers' = 2/3. (Trap answer 60 comes from forgetting to renormalize and using 2/4.) Any 'survivors of two carriers' problem hides this same renormalization.

cards.title: The classic distractor pairs — know the split cold
cards.body:
- **Carrier $2pq$ vs. allele frequency $q$** — the #1 HW trap. 'Carriers/heterozygotes' = $2pq$, roughly double $q$ for a rare allele.
- **Frameshift vs. point/in-frame** — an indel **not** a multiple of 3 = **frameshift**; a multiple of 3 keeps the reading frame. (Tay-Sachs 4-bp insertion → frameshift.)
- **Huntington's (autosomal DOMINANT) vs. albinism/PKU/Tay-Sachs (recessive)** — Huntington's is the odd-one-out on 'which are autosomal recessive.' Enzyme-deficiency (loss-of-function) diseases are almost all recessive; Huntington's is a late-onset gain-of-function CAG-repeat disease.
- **X-linked recessive vs. mitochondrial vs. Y-linked** — mito = mother→ALL; Y = father→sons only; X-linked recessive = no father-to-son, skips.
- **Aneuploidy (Down 47, Turner 45, Klinefelter XXY 47 — change count) vs. deletion/imprinting (Cri-du-chat 5p⁻, Prader-Willi/Angelman 15q — normal count 46, structural)** — the 'normal chromosome number' karyotype question turns on this. In ONE patient, Turner ($-1$) + Down ($+1$) can net back to 46.
- **Odd polyploid (triploid = sterile/seedless) vs. even polyploid (tetraploid = fertile)** — sterility comes from *odd* ploidy: an odd number of homolog sets can't pair evenly in meiosis.
- **Z-linked (birds: ZW females are the affected/hemizygous sex) vs. X-linked (mammals: XY males)** — flip the sex.

cards.title: Mutation types & modified dihybrid ratios
cards.body:
**Mutations by effect:**
- **Frameshift** = insertion/deletion NOT a multiple of 3 (shifts every downstream codon).
- **Trinucleotide/triplet repeat expansion** → **anticipation** (disease onset earlier / worse each generation as the repeat grows) — Huntington's, Fragile X, myotonic dystrophy. Buzz: 'gets worse every generation.'

**Epistasis / modified dihybrid ratios (baseline 9:3:3:1):**
- **15:1** → **duplicate dominant** genes: two genes redundantly make the same product, so a dominant allele at *either* locus suffices; only the 1/16 double-recessive lacks it → parallel/redundant pathways.
- **9:7** (duplicate recessive) or **9:3:4** (recessive epistasis) → genes act in the **same pathway**; a homozygous-recessive block at one locus masks the other.

Recognizing the ratio tells you the gene-interaction architecture — that's the whole point of the question.

memorize.trigger: Recombination frequency for genes on different chromosomes
'Passes to ALL her children, none of his' inheritance
'Disease gets worse / onset earlier every generation' = anticipation
Indel that is NOT a multiple of 3
Seedless / weak seeds from meiotic pairing problems
Which of albinism / PKU / Huntington's is NOT autosomal recessive
Surviving offspring of two carriers of a lethal recessive → fraction that are carriers
memorize.answer: 2/3 (renormalize 1:2:1 to 1:2 after removing the dead aa)

memorize.trigger: Birds/reptiles sex chromosomes; which sex is hemizygous
memorize.answer: Males ZZ, females ZW — the FEMALE (ZW) is hemizygous
Duplicate dominant genes — two loci redundantly make the same product (either dominant suffices)

memorize.trigger: Coefficient of relatedness: full sibs / parent-offspring

practice.note: Pure $3^n$ rule. 'Heterozygous for 4 distinct traits,' self-cross → they want the number of GENOTYPES, not phenotypes. Don't confuse $3^n$ (genotypes) with $2^n$ (phenotypes).
practice.solution: Each heterozygous locus ($Aa \times Aa$) yields 3 genotypes (AA, Aa, aa). Four independently assorting loci → $3^4 = 81$ possible genotypes. Answer: 81.

practice.note: Textbook Hardy-Weinberg carrier problem — and the #1 trap. They ask for HETEROZYGOTES, so the answer is $2pq$, not $q$. Square-root the prevalence first.

Lethal recessive → condition on survival. The aa quarter dies before birth, so it's not among the 120 'children' — renormalize over the surviving 3 classes. (Trap answer 60 = forgetting to renormalize.)
practice.solution: $Aa \times Aa$ gives 1 AA: 2 Aa: 1 aa, but aa die before birth, so the 120 are the survivors (1 AA: 2 Aa). Carriers are 2/3 of them: $120 \times 2/3 = 80$. Answer: 80.

practice.note: Inheritance-pattern recognition. A woman passes the trait to ALL six of her children while her brother passes it to NONE of his 54 — only females transmit, and to every child. Rule out Y-linked (father→sons) and Mendelian patterns.
practice.solution: Maternal-only transmission to every child is the signature of mitochondrial inheritance (mitochondria come only from the egg). The brother, being male, transmits none. Answer: Y) Mitochondrial.

practice.note: Karyotype counting — aneuploidy (changes chromosome number) vs. deletion/imprinting (normal number, 46). One patient carrying TWO conditions: find the pair whose count changes cancel. Klinefelter (+1) and Down (+1) add; Turner (−1) subtracts; cri-du-chat / Prader-Willi / Angelman are structural (still 46).
practice.solution: A single patient with both Turner (monosomy X, −1) and Down (trisomy 21, +1): starting from 46, the −1 and +1 cancel → 46, a normal count. The other options pair a count-changing aneuploidy with either another aneuploidy (nets 47/45) or a structural disorder that doesn't cancel it. Answer: Y) Turner and Down.

practice.note: Z-linked Hardy-Weinberg with a twist — females are the hemizygous sex (ZW), so affected-female frequency gives $q$ directly (no square root). Then find P(carrier | phenotypically normal male).
practice.solution: Females (ZW) show the trait with one allele, so affected-female frequency $= q = 0.2$; $p = 0.8$. Males are ZZ: normal males are $Z^A Z^A$ ($p^2 = 0.64$) or carriers $Z^A Z^a$ ($2pq = 0.32$). P(carrier | normal male) $= \frac{2pq}{p^2 + 2pq} = \frac{0.32}{0.96} = \frac{1}{3}$. Answer: 1/3.

subject: bio

why: Plant Biology is one of the densest and most predictable bio clusters in the bank — 47 questions (13.6% of bio) that recycle the same handful of hormone, tissue, and reproduction facts every year, so a small amount of well-structured study buys a large number of buzzes.
overview:
Plant Biology is the highest-yield-per-hour topic in the bio bank: **47 questions, ~14% of all bio**, and they orbit a tiny set of recurring themes. Learn the **core hormones**, the **three ground tissues**, **flower/seed anatomy + ploidy**, and the **soil/transport vocabulary**, and you can buzz on the large majority of these.

How it shows up in Science Bowl:
- **Hormone ID** (~1/3 of questions): "which hormone closes stomata / makes rice topple / gives the triple response?" These are pure trigger-word reflexes.
- **Anatomy ID**: name the tissue or structure from a one-line description (celery crunch → collenchyma; lateral roots → pericycle; apple flesh → receptacle).
- **Reproduction**: ABC model whorl shifts, endosperm 3n, gametophytic self-incompatibility, megagametophyte cell names.
- **Nutrition/transport**: Casparian strip, cation exchange, transpiration, C4 compartmentation.
- **Phylogeny**: bryophytes, ferns, vascular-plant derived traits, phragmoplast cytokinesis.

Formats lean hard on "**which is LEAST/NOT**" and "**identify all that are TRUE**," so you need clean either/or distinctions, not vibes — a fuzzy sense of a fact will fail a "select all" question.

The smartest way to learn this is **not** isolated flashcards. Build the plant's **cause-and-effect story**: a hormone is defined by the phenotype it causes, a tissue by whether it's alive and lignified, a structure by where water or genes flow through it. Anchor every fact to a mechanism ("ethylene = triple response = short, thick, horizontal") and the recall drills itself.

cards.title: The core plant hormones by signature phenotype
cards.body:
A hormone is defined by what it *causes* — memorize the phenotype, not the molecule.
- **Auxin** → cell elongation (acid growth); phototropism/gravitropism; drives apical dominance.
- **Cytokinin** → cell *division*; **delays senescence** (stays-green); **promotes axillary/lateral bud outgrowth** (opposes auxin); made in roots. High **cytokinin:auxin ratio → shoots**, low → roots in tissue culture.
- **Gibberellin (GA)** → stem elongation + breaks dormancy → germination.
- **Abscisic acid (ABA)** → stress/dormancy: closes stomata, inhibits germination.
- **Ethylene** → triple response (short, thick, horizontal) + fruit ripening.
- **Strigolactones** → inhibit axillary buds (reinforce apical dominance) + attract mycorrhizae.
- **Jasmonates** → wound response + defense vs **herbivores/necrotrophs** (5-carbon cyclopentanone ring, from linolenic acid).
- **Salicylic acid** → **SAR** (systemic acquired resistance vs biotrophs); **methyl salicylate = the mobile signal**.

**Antagonist pairs to lock in:** ABA vs GA (dormancy vs germination); auxin vs cytokinin (apical dominance vs lateral-bud release). **High auxin backfires**: above ~0.1 mM it induces ethylene, which *inhibits* growth.

cards.title: WHY auxin elongation needs expansins (acid growth)
cards.body:
Auxin doesn't stretch the wall directly — it runs a two-step mechanism:
1. Auxin activates a **proton pump** → dumps $H^+$ into the cell wall, dropping wall pH.
2. Low pH activates **expansins**, proteins that break the hydrogen bonds gluing cellulose microfibrils together → the wall 'creeps' and the turgid cell elongates.

So the buzz chain is **proton pump + loosens cell wall → expansins** (mechanism = auxin's acid growth). This is the engine behind phototropism and gravitropism. If a question names the proton pump and asks *what breaks the H-bonds*, the answer is expansins, not auxin.

cards.title: WHY endosperm is 3n and the megagametophyte layout
cards.body:
**Double fertilization**: one sperm ($n$) fuses with the egg → **zygote 2n**; the *second* sperm ($n$) fuses with the central cell's **two polar nuclei** ($n+n$) → **endosperm 3n**. So endosperm = 3× the haploid number. If a cell has $n=11$, endosperm $=33$.

The mature megagametophyte (Polygonum type) has **8 nuclei / 7 cells**: the egg, **2 synergids** (flank the egg, guide the pollen tube via filiform apparatus), **3 antipodal cells** (at the far *chalazal* end), and the central cell with 2 polar nuclei. 'Three cells at the chalazal end' → **antipodals**; 'flank the egg / guide pollen tube' → **synergids**. Every cell here is haploid, so any given chromosome count IS the $n$ value.

cards.title: Three ground tissues: alive-vs-dead is the whole game
cards.body:
The dividing line is **living status + lignification**:
- **Parenchyma** — alive, thin-walled (the generalist: photosynthesis, storage).
- **Collenchyma** — alive, flexible; **living support** that bends (the crunch of celery, angular corner-thickened primary walls, NO lignin).
- **Sclerenchyma** — **DEAD at maturity**, lignified secondary walls; rigid support (fibers + sclereids = nutshells, cherry pit, gritty pear stone cells). **Stains red with phloroglucinol-HCl** (Wiesner test) because lignin is present.

Question tells: 'alive' → collenchyma; 'dead + lignified + stains red' → sclerenchyma. Lignin is the single tell for sclerenchyma.

cards.title: Buzz words → instant answer
cards.body:
- 'closes stomata / inhibits germination / acidic / imbibition washes out' → **ABA**
- 'short, thick, horizontal / triple response / high auxin induces' → **ethylene**
- 'foolish seedling / rice topples / too tall' → **gibberellins**
- 'delays leaf senescence / promotes cell division / made in roots / releases lateral buds' → **cytokinin**
- 'proton pump + loosens wall / breaks H-bonds' → **expansins**
- 'attracts mycorrhizae + inhibits axillary buds' → **strigolactones**
- '5-carbon cyclopentanone ring lipid / made from linolenic acid / herbivore & wound defense' → **jasmonates**
- 'SAR / systemic acquired resistance / methyl salicylate is the mobile signal' → **salicylic acid** (NOT jasmonate)
- 'lateral roots originate from' → **pericycle**
- 'settles by gravity / starch grains / statolith' → **amyloplast** (never just 'plastid')
- 'root pressure pushes water out of leaf' → **guttation**
- 'apple flesh from' → **receptacle**; 'modified leaves attracting pollinators' → **bracts**

cards.title: Worked buzz: the double-negative ethylene question
cards.body:
*Clue:* 'A mutant grows shorter, thicker, more horizontal than wild type. Which mutation is consistent?'

Step 1: short + thick + horizontal = **triple response = active ethylene signaling** (the phenotype of a plant sensing ethylene).

Step 2: you want a mutation that turns ethylene signaling **ON constitutively**. Options: loss of ethylene *receptor* (→ would kill signaling, wrong), overproduce ABA (wrong hormone), kill an ABA kinase (wrong hormone), or **loss-of-function of an INHIBITOR of ethylene signaling** (e.g. a CTR1-like repressor).

Step 3: knocking out an inhibitor *releases the brake* → signaling runs constitutively → triple response. **Answer: loss-of-function of an ethylene-signaling inhibitor.** Watch for the double negative — 'loss of an inhibitor' = gain of pathway.

cards.title: Roots, soil, and transport vocabulary
cards.body:
- **Casparian strip** (classic textbook answer: **suberin**; also lignin) waterproofs the endodermis → blocks the apoplast → forces water into the **symplastic** route so minerals cross a selective membrane. If lignin is already named, the other answer is **suberin**.
- **Cation exchange**: roots pump $H^+$ to displace mineral cations ($K^+$, $Ca^{2+}$) off negatively-charged clay/humus. **Acidifying soil** frees metal cations ($Al$, $Fe$) — but makes **phosphate LESS available** (it binds Al/Fe).
- **Nitrogen deficiency shows on OLDER leaves first** — N is mobile, so the plant reallocates it to new growth. (Same for the mobile nutrients Mg, K, P.)
- **Transpiration is DECREASED** by high humidity and by ABA (closes stomata); **guttation** is the *opposite* (push from root pressure, not transpirational pull).

cards.title: Classic distractor pairs — keep these straight
cards.body:
- **Collenchyma vs sclerenchyma** — living/flexible/no-lignin vs dead/rigid/lignified. 'Alive' → collenchyma.
- **Modified STEM vs ROOT** — rhizomes, tubers (potato), stolons, corms = **stems**; **pneumatophores** and taproots = **roots** (the trap in 'which is NOT a modified stem').
- **Auxin low vs high** — low = elongation; high (>0.1 mM) = triggers ethylene = inhibition.
- **ABA vs gibberellin** — dormancy vs germination; antagonists. **Auxin vs cytokinin** — apical dominance vs lateral-bud release.
- **Jasmonate vs salicylic acid** — JA = wound/herbivore/necrotroph defense; SA = SAR + methyl salicylate. Do NOT assign SAR to jasmonate.
- **Monocot vs eudicot** — *scattered* vascular bundles + fibrous roots + parallel veins = **monocot**; ringed bundles + taproot + net veins = **eudicot**. 'Eudicot stems have scattered bundles' is **FALSE**.
- **Endosperm 3n vs zygote 2n** — multiply given $n$ by 3 for endosperm.
- **C4 compartments** — **PEP carboxylase** in the *mesophyll* (fixes CO2 first into 4-C oxaloacetate); **Rubisco + concentrated CO2** in the *bundle sheath*.

cards.title: ABC model, MADS-box, and self-incompatibility
cards.body:
**ABC model** of flower whorls (outer→inner): A→sepals, A+B→petals, B+C→stamens, C→carpels. **A and C are mutually antagonistic**, so **lose gene C and A spreads** into its whorls → **sepal-petal-petal-sepal** (reproductive parts revert to sterile perianth organs). These are **MADS-box** genes (AGAMOUS = C, DEFICIENS = B) — homeotic like animal HOX but a completely separate gene family, named for a conserved DNA-binding domain (MCM1/AGAMOUS/DEFICIENS/SRF).

**Gametophytic self-incompatibility**: pollen is rejected if its *own haploid* S-allele matches *either* maternal allele. An S1S2 mother accepts pollen only from a father supplying a non-matching allele — e.g. **S2S3 pollen works** because the haploid S3 tube differs from both S1 and S2 (the S2 grains are rejected, but S3 gets through). Contrast **sporophytic** SI, where the pollen's behavior is set by the *diploid parent's* genotype, so S2S3 would be fully rejected.

cards.title: Phylogeny cause-and-effect: where the traits appear
cards.body:
Think of plant evolution as adding features in order:
- **Charophytes + land plants** share the **phragmoplast** (cell-plate) mode of cytokinesis → distinguishes them from **chlorophytes and red algae** (which divide by furrowing/other modes). Under a tubulin/DAPI stain, chlorophytes and red algae look different from charophytes; land plants match the charophytes.
- **Bryophytes (mosses)** are transitional: **hydroids ≈ proto-xylem, leptoids ≈ proto-phloem**, but *no true lignified vascular tissue*. **Liverworts are among the earliest-diverging land plants** (predate vascular plants).
- **Derived vascular-plant traits** are tricky in 'select all': **vessel elements are NOT a universal trait of all vascular plants** (most ferns and gymnosperms have only tracheids; vessels are mainly angiosperms + gnetophytes), so 'identify the derived characteristic shared by ALL vascular plants' often answers 'lignified tracheids / true vascular tissue,' not vessels.
- Inclusiveness nesting: **Viridiplantae (green algae + land plants) ⊃ Streptophyta (charophytes + land plants) ⊃ Embryophyta (= 'Plantae' in the land-plant sense).**

Triple response: short, thick, horizontal (and high auxin induces it)
Foolish seedling disease / rice grows too tall and topples
Promotes cell division, delays leaf senescence, made in roots, releases axillary buds (opposes auxin)
Proton pump into cell wall, then H-bonds between cellulose microfibrils are broken by...
Attracts mycorrhizae + inhibits axillary bud growth (promoted by auxin)
5-carbon cyclopentanone-ring lipid from linolenic acid / wound + herbivore/necrotroph defense
Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) / methyl salicylate is the mobile long-distance signal
Lateral roots originate from this structure
Dead at maturity, lignified secondary walls, stains red with phloroglucinol-HCl
Statoliths that sense gravity are a specialized version of this starch-storing organelle
Root pressure forces water out of the leaf → what phenomenon
Most of the flesh of an apple comes from this structure
Casparian strip's key waterproofing constituent (classic answer)
memorize.answer: Suberin — forces water into the symplastic route

memorize.trigger: Lose gene C in the ABC model → whorl pattern
Cell-plate mode of cytokinesis shared by charophytes + land plants

practice.note: Textbook ABA hormone-ID. Three clues stacked: imbibition washes it out, it closes stomata, and it's acidic. Any one alone is enough to buzz — don't wait for all three.
practice.solution: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the stress/dormancy hormone. It enforces seed dormancy (so water uptake/imbibition dilutes and washes it out to *permit* germination), closes stomata under drought, and is literally an acid. All three descriptors point uniquely to ABA. Stored answer: Abscisic Acid (ABA).

practice.note: The double-negative trap. Short/thick/horizontal = the ethylene triple response, so you need a mutation that turns ethylene signaling ON. The answer is loss of an INHIBITOR, not loss of the receptor.
practice.solution: The triple-response phenotype means ethylene signaling is active. Choice W (loss of the ethylene *receptor*) would abolish signaling — wrong direction. Y and Z are the wrong hormone (ABA). Choice X, a loss-of-function mutation in an *inhibitor* of ethylene signal transduction, removes the brake, so the pathway runs constitutively → constant triple response. Stored answer: X.

practice.note: Ploidy arithmetic. The synergids are part of the haploid megagametophyte (n = 11), so this is really '3 × n'. The synergid detail just hands you the haploid number.
practice.solution: Synergids are cells of the haploid female gametophyte, so n = 11. Endosperm forms when the second sperm (n) fuses with the two polar nuclei (n + n) during double fertilization → 3n. Therefore endosperm = 3 × 11 = 33 chromosomes. Stored answer: 33.

practice.note: ABC-model whorl shift. Loss of C lets A spread into C's territory. Because A and C are mutually antagonistic, the two inner whorls revert. Map it before answering.
practice.solution: Wild type outer→inner is sepal-petal-stamen-carpel (A, A+B, B+C, C). Losing C removes C activity and, since A and C are antagonists, A expands into all four whorls: A, A+B, A+B, A = sepal, petal, petal, sepal. Stored answer: Y) Sepal-petal-petal-sepal.

practice.note: Ground-tissue ID by stacked tells: lignified + secondary walls + dead at maturity + stains red with phloroglucinol-HCl. Any of these screams sclerenchyma; collenchyma is the 'alive' distractor.
practice.solution: Phloroglucinol-HCl (Wiesner test) staining red indicates lignin. Sclerenchyma is the only ground tissue that is dead at maturity with thick, lignified secondary walls (fibers and sclereids). Parenchyma and collenchyma are alive and non-lignified; aerenchyma is air-space tissue. Stored answer: Z) Sclerenchyma.

practice.note: Two-part self-incompatibility question. First nail the TYPE (gametophytic vs sporophytic), then apply the allele-matching rule — the rule differs between the two SI systems.
practice.solution: For fertilization to succeed against an S1S2 pistil, the mother must be able to accept some pollen. Under *gametophytic* SI the pollen's fate is set by its own *haploid* S-allele, so from an S2S3 father the S2 grains are rejected but the S3 grains (allele absent in the mother) grow and fertilize. Under *sporophytic* SI the diploid father's genotype governs, so any S2S3 pollen would be wholly rejected. Hence the answer must be gametophytic with S2S3 pollen. Stored answer: Z) Gametophytic, S2S3.

subject: bio

why: Anatomy & Physiology is the single largest bio bank (~18% of questions), and it rewards pathway thinking: once you own a handful of ordered sequences and feedback loops, the recurring 'order these events' and 'NOT true' formats become nearly free points.
overview:
**What this covers.** Human and comparative-animal organ systems: cardiovascular, endocrine, digestive, respiratory/blood-gas, muscle, and kidney/osmoregulation, plus a steady trickle of comparative-physiology curveballs (birds, insects, sharks, fish).

**How it shows up.** Two clusters dominate and together make up roughly half the bank: **the heart** (SA node, conduction order, cardiac cycle, valves, PV loops, intercalated discs, RAAS/ANP) and **the endocrine system** (hypothalamus→pituitary→gland axis, thyroid, steroid vs. peptide hormones, the POMC/ACTH family). Digestion, hemoglobin/blood-gas transport, and muscle physiology fill most of the rest. The formats are distinctive: lots of "**order these 3–4 events**" (cardiac cycle, digestive enzymes, blood-vessel sequence), "**identify all that are true**" multi-selects, and "**NOT true**" negation tossups where one plausible-sounding line is the trap.

**Smartest way to learn it.** Don't memorize organs in isolation — learn the **pathways and feedback loops as stories**. Trace one drop of blood through the heart and lungs, one bite of food down the gut, one signal from hypothalamus to target gland. Once you own each sequence, every ordering question is automatic. Then bolt on the ~15 "trigger-term" facts (aromatase, inhibin, thermogenin, hemocyanin, ryanodine receptor) that are pure one-to-one name recalls. Finally, drill the classic distractor pairs (sigmoidal vs. hyperbolic, steroid vs. peptide, fetal vs. adult Hb) because that's exactly where the negation traps live.

cards.title: The cardiac conduction pathway (own this order)
cards.body:
**SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers.** The SA node sits in the **right atrium** and sets the heart's rate — it's the pacemaker.

- Signal fires at the SA node, spreads across the atria, pauses at the AV node (lets atria finish filling ventricles), races down the His bundle through the septum, then out the Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles **apex-first (bottom-up)** so blood is squeezed toward the outflow valves.
- **Answer 'sinoatrial node,' NEVER 'pacemaker'** — the bank explicitly rejects the descriptive word.
- The SA node's spontaneous firing comes from **HCN / 'funny' (F-type) channels** (the I_f current) that leak Na⁺ inward and slowly self-depolarize the cell, so any 'F-type receptor / funny channel' clue points straight to the SA node.

cards.title: The cardiac cycle, PV loop, and heart sounds
cards.body:
Order: **ventricular filling → mitral valve closes → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation.**

- **Isovolumetric** = both valves shut, volume constant, pressure changing. There are two such phases (one contracting, one relaxing).
- On a pressure–volume loop, start where the mitral valve opens (filling); **end-diastolic volume ≈ 120 mL** is read off the right side of the loop.
- **Heart sounds map onto the cycle:** **S1 ('lub') = AV (mitral + tricuspid) valves snapping shut** at the start of systole; **S2 ('dub') = semilunar (aortic + pulmonic) valves shutting** at the start of diastole.
- The **left ventricle has the thickest myocardium** because it pumps to the whole body (systemic circuit); the right ventricle only pushes blood on the short trip to the lungs.

cards.title: WHY hemoglobin is sigmoidal but myoglobin is hyperbolic
cards.body:
Hemoglobin has **4 subunits that cooperate**: the first O₂ that binds makes the next bind easier (positive cooperativity), so the saturation curve is **S-shaped (sigmoidal)**. That shape means Hb loads O₂ hard in the lungs and dumps it readily in tissues — an efficient delivery truck.

- **Myoglobin has 1 subunit** — nothing to cooperate with — so it grabs O₂ tightly and holds it: a **hyperbolic** curve. It's a storage tank in muscle, not a delivery truck.
- **Bohr effect (the WHY tissues get more O₂):** high CO₂ / low pH in active tissue shifts the Hb curve **right** (lower affinity), so Hb unloads O₂ exactly where it's needed; the lungs (low CO₂, high pH) shift it back left to reload.
- **Fetal Hb has HIGHER O₂ affinity** than adult, because it must pull O₂ *from* maternal blood across the placenta (it binds 2,3-BPG poorly, which is why its curve sits left).
- At **high altitude** the body raises hematocrit, EPO, and **2,3-BPG** (which shifts the adult curve right to unload more O₂ in tissues).

cards.title: WHY RAAS and ANP are a blood-pressure tug-of-war
cards.body:
Think of it as two opposing teams:

- **RAAS RAISES pressure.** Low BP → kidney releases **renin** → angiotensin I → (via **ACE**) angiotensin II, a **vasoconstrictor** → triggers **aldosterone** → kidney retains Na⁺ and water → more blood volume, higher BP.
- **ANP LOWERS pressure.** When the atria are stretched by high volume, they release **atrial natriuretic peptide** → promotes Na⁺ **excretion** → less volume, lower BP. ANP **inhibits** the whole RAAS.
- **ACE inhibitors** (lisinopril / Zestril) block angiotensin II formation to lower BP.
- The signature **NOT-true trap**: "ANP *increases* aldosterone release" — false; it does the opposite.

cards.title: Steroid vs. peptide hormones & the hypothalamus axis
cards.body:
**Steroids cross the phospholipid bilayer and bind intracellular (cytoplasmic/nuclear) receptors; peptides bind surface receptors.**

- Steroids are cholesterol-derived and lipid-soluble, so they slip through membranes and act by changing gene transcription (slow, lasting). **Aldosterone and cortisol are steroids** (cortisol from the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex). 'Crosses to a cytoplasmic receptor' = steroid = aldosterone.
- Peptides can't cross the membrane, so they bind surface receptors and work through **second messengers** (cAMP, etc.) — fast, short-lived.
- The **hypothalamus** secretes releasing hormones (**TRH, CRH, GHRH**) and connects to the posterior pituitary via the **infundibulum**; the **median eminence** feeds the hypothalamic–pituitary portal system that carries releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary.
- **Prolactin is the exception** — under *tonic inhibition*: **dopamine inhibits it, TRH stimulates it**, so it's both positively and negatively regulated.
- **POMC (pro-opiomelanocortin)** is cleaved into **ACTH and MSH** — so 'same precursor as ACTH' = MSH, not vasopressin or melatonin.

cards.title: Digestion: the enzyme order and lipid pathway
cards.body:
Follow the food. **Salivary amylase (mouth) → pepsin (stomach) → trypsin (small intestine).**

- **Zymogens** are inactive enzyme precursors activated by cleavage: **enterokinase (enteropeptidase) cleaves trypsinogen → trypsin**, which then activates the other pancreatic proteases (this cascade keeps the pancreas from digesting itself).
- **Parietal cells** make HCl and **intrinsic factor** (for B12 absorption); **chief cells** make pepsinogen. Don't swap them.
- **CCK** triggers bile *release* and pancreatic enzyme secretion, inhibits gastric emptying, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi — it does NOT cause bile *synthesis* (the liver synthesizes bile continuously).
- **Lipid order:** bile salts **emulsify → chylomicrons assemble → enter circulation via lymph** (lacteals), bypassing the hepatic portal vein. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate → **hypervitaminosis** (Vitamin A is the go-to answer); water-soluble (B, C) are peed out.

cards.title: Buzz words → instant answers
cards.body:
- "Sets the rate," "right atrium," "F-type / funny channel" → **SA node** (say sinoatrial)
- "Crosses the bilayer / cytoplasmic receptor" → **steroid** (aldosterone, cortisol)
- "Infundibulum," "releasing hormones," "median eminence" → **hypothalamus**
- "Same precursor as ACTH," "POMC" → **MSH**
- "Inhibits FSH," "Sertoli cells" → **inhibin**
- "Androgen → estrogen," "theca cells" → **aromatase**
- "Converts CO₂ + water in RBCs" → **carbonic anhydrase**
- "Proton-leak channel," "brown fat," "nonshivering thermogenesis" → **thermogenin / UCP1**
- "Copper pigment in insect hemolymph" → **hemocyanin**
- "Named for a plant alkaloid, releases Ca²⁺ from the SR" → **ryanodine receptor**
- "Vasoconstrictor made by ACE" → **angiotensin II**; "atria release to oppose RAAS" → **ANP**
- "Hibernation + estivation" → **torpor**; "open system, fluid in the hemocoel" → **hemolymph**

cards.title: Worked buzz — the F-type receptor clue
cards.body:
**Clue:** "An inhibitor is made for the **F-type receptor** and used on the heart. Which region has the most F-type receptors?"

**How to land it fast:** 'F-type' = 'funny' = **HCN channels**, the pacemaker current that lets cells depolarize spontaneously. The region that *self-fires* to set the rate is the **SA node** (right atrium). The AV node, His bundle, and Purkinje fibers conduct but don't normally set the pace.

**Answer: Z) SA node.** Same reflex works for 'sets the timing / right atrium / pacemaker current' — all roads lead to the sinoatrial node (and remember: never say 'pacemaker' as your spoken answer).

cards.title: Classic distractor pairs (know the split)
cards.body:
- **Sigmoidal vs. hyperbolic** → hemoglobin (cooperative, 4 subunits) vs. myoglobin (1 subunit).
- **Fetal vs. adult Hb** → fetal has **HIGHER** O₂ affinity.
- **Steroid vs. peptide** → intracellular receptor vs. surface receptor.
- **Thyroid vs. adrenal** → Graves' (hyper) and myxedema (hypo) are thyroid; **Addison's is adrenal** — don't lump it in with thyroid disorders.
- **Parietal cells** (HCl + intrinsic factor) vs. **chief cells** (pepsinogen).
- **Fat-soluble A,D,E,K** (hypervitaminosis) vs. **water-soluble B,C** (excreted).
- **Veins have THINNER walls than arteries** (bigger lumen, less elastic tissue) — the NOT-true line always claims veins are thicker.
- **Birds:** nucleated RBCs, **cross-current** exchange with unidirectional air-sac flow (highly efficient) — the trap says birds use simple tidal/positive-pressure breathing (false). Don't confuse with fish gills, which use **counter-current**.
- **ANP inhibits RAAS** — the trap says ANP increases aldosterone (false).

cards.title: Comparative & excretory trigger terms that trip people up
cards.body:
- **Excretory systems:** flatworms → **flame cells**; annelids AND molluscs → **metanephridia**; insects → **Malpighian tubules**. The trap is calling 'mollusc + metanephridia' wrong — it's actually correct.
- **Sharks retain urea** (buffered by **TMAO**) to stay slightly hyperosmotic to seawater — the nitrogenous 'waste' they deliberately keep.
- **Kidney osmolarity is highest deep in the medulla at the Loop of Henle** (countercurrent multiplier builds a salty gradient); **ADH** inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct to reabsorb water down that gradient.
- **Insects:** breathe through **tracheae** (rings held open by **chitin**) directly to tissues; open circulation, **hemolymph** in the hemocoel, copper-based **hemocyanin** (the bank's stated pigment for insect hemolymph).
- **Muscle:** intercalated discs = **desmosomes + gap junctions** (heart contracts as a syncytium, gap junctions passing the signal cell-to-cell); myosin-ATPase speed **smooth < cardiac < skeletal**; smooth muscle's dense bodies ≈ skeletal Z discs.

memorize.answer: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers
S1 = AV (mitral+tricuspid) valves close; S2 = semilunar (aortic+pulmonic) valves close

memorize.trigger: Hormone that crosses the bilayer to a cytoplasmic receptor
Hormone both positively AND negatively regulated by hypothalamus
Inhibits FSH, released by Sertoli cells
Enzyme converting androgens to estrogens (theca cells, per bank)
Atria release this to oppose RAAS / Na+ reabsorption
Enzyme making bicarbonate from CO2 + water in RBCs
Hb vs. myoglobin O2-saturation curve shapes
Copper respiratory pigment in insect hemolymph

practice.note: 'F-type receptor' is the whole clue — map it to the pacemaker current, not to a conduction relay.
practice.solution: F-type ('funny'/HCN) channels drive spontaneous depolarization, and the region that self-fires to set the heart's rate is the SA node (right atrium). AV node, His bundle, and Purkinje fibers conduct but don't set the pace. Answer: Z) SA Node.

practice.note: An ordering question — trace one drop of blood starting at the right ventricle, and don't forget the systemic detour to the gut.
practice.solution: From the right ventricle: blood goes out the pulmonary ARTERY (2) to the lungs first, returns via the pulmonary VEIN (1) to the left heart, then is pumped systemically — the hepatic portal vein (3), draining the gut to the liver, is reached last. Answer: 2, 1, 3.

practice.note: Match curve shape to subunit count: cooperativity makes an S-curve, a single site makes a simple curve.
practice.solution: Hemoglobin's 4 cooperating subunits give a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve for efficient load/unload; single-subunit myoglobin binds O2 tightly with a hyperbolic curve. Answer: Y) Sigmoidal, hyperbolic.

practice.note: Follow the food through the tract, not the numbered order given in the list.
practice.solution: Salivary amylase acts in the mouth, pepsin in the acidic stomach, trypsin in the small intestine. Given 1) amylase, 2) trypsin, 3) pepsin, the chronological order is 1, 3, 2.

practice.note: A 'NOT true' negation tossup — three lines describe RAAS correctly; find the one that reverses ANP's role.
practice.solution: ANP opposes RAAS: it promotes Na+ excretion and inhibits aldosterone, so the claim that 'ANP increases aldosterone release by the adrenal glands' is false. The other three (low BP → renin, aldosterone → Na+ reabsorption, ACE inhibitors lower BP) are all correct. Answer: Z.

practice.note: 'Identify all' multi-select keyed on shared precursor — only cleavage products of POMC count.
practice.solution: ACTH is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), and so is MSH — but vasopressin (a posterior-pituitary peptide) and melatonin (from the pineal, a tryptophan derivative) are not. Only MSH shares the precursor. Answer: 3 ONLY.

subject: bio

why: This topic is ~3% of the bio bank and is high-leverage because every question reduces to one mental model — the animal tree of life. Once you can draw the tree and hang traits on the branches, the "identify-all-true," "which-is-NOT," and "order-these" formats all fall out mechanically instead of as dozens of disconnected flashcards. The distinctions tested (protostome/deuterostome, coelom types, nested vertebrate clades) recur verbatim across years, so a small study investment pays off repeatedly.
overview:
## What this topic covers

**Animal Diversity & Taxonomy is the animal tree of life** — sorting animals into phyla by diagnostic traits, and reading the branching order of the major clades. In Science Bowl it shows up in three recurring flavors:

1. **"Name the phylum from a clue."** A signature cell or structure is given, you buzz the phylum: *nematocysts* → Cnidaria, *choanocytes/collar cells* → Porifera.
2. **Body-plan grades along the tree.** Protostome vs deuterostome (blastopore fate, cleavage type), presence of a true coelom, Bilateria membership, and which phyla are "least related." Almost always *identify-all-that-are-true* or *which-is-NOT* formats.
3. **Vertebrate evolution.** The nested chordate clades and the **order traits appeared**: mineralized skeleton → jaws → digited limbs → amniotic egg — plus fish-physiology curveballs (TMAO, spiral valve, lateral line).

## How to learn it the smart way

**Draw the tree once, then hang traits on the branches.** Every question is secretly asking *"where on the tree does this feature sit, and what's nested inside what?"* If you know the branching order and the single trait that defines each fork, the mechanical formats solve themselves.

The writers trap you by **swapping paired attributes** (protostome cleavage is spiral, not radial) and **reversing containment direction** (Bilateria contains Protostomia, never the reverse). So don't just memorize facts — memorize them *as pairs with their distractor*, and always check the direction of "contains."

cards.title: The one tree everything hangs on
cards.body:
Walk from the animal root outward, and each fork is defined by **one** innovation:

- **Porifera** (sponges) branch first — no true tissues.
- **Cnidaria/Ctenophora** — radial, **diploblastic** (2 germ layers, no mesoderm), *outside* Bilateria.
- **Bilateria** — bilateral symmetry + **mesoderm** (triploblastic). Splits into:
 - **Protostomia** (mouth-first) → *Ecdysozoa* (molters: Arthropoda, Nematoda) + *Lophotrochozoa* (Mollusca, Annelida, Rotifera)
 - **Deuterostomia** (anus-first) → only **3 phyla**: Echinodermata, Chordata, Hemichordata

Know this skeleton and you can answer 'least related,' 'which is NOT a protostome,' and 'contains' questions by inspection.

cards.title: WHY mesoderm is the master fork
cards.body:
Mesoderm (the third germ layer) is what separates simple animals from complex ones. No mesoderm → **no true coelom** (a coelom is a cavity *fully lined by mesoderm*) and no bilateral body plan.

That single fact chains together three separate test answers:
- Jellyfish (Cnidaria) are **diploblastic** → no mesoderm → **no coelom** and radial, not bilateral.
- That's also *why* Cnidaria is 'least related to Arthropoda' — it sits **outside Bilateria** entirely.

So when you see 'diploblastic,' immediately think: radial, no coelom, pre-Bilaterian. One mechanism, many buzzes.

cards.title: WHY the vertebrate trait order is not arbitrary
cards.body:
The order **mineralized skeleton → jaws → digited limbs → amniotic egg** is just the tree read from fish toward mammals. Each trait defines a *deeper-nested* clade:

- Bone appears in early vertebrates.
- Jaws define **Gnathostomata** (inside vertebrates).
- Digited limbs define **Tetrapoda** (inside gnathostomes).
- The amniotic egg defines **Amniota** (inside tetrapods) — the innovation that **freed vertebrates from water** to reproduce, so it's LAST/most-derived.

You never memorize the sequence as four floating facts — you read it off the nesting. Amniotic egg in an ordering question is almost always the last trait.

cards.title: Coelom, pseudocoelom, acoelom
cards.body:
A body-cavity classification the bank tests via 'which have a true coelom' lists:

- **True coelom (eucoelomate):** cavity *fully lined by mesoderm* — annelids, molluscs, chordates, and arthropods. **Honey bee = YES.** (Arthropods are classed as coelomates developmentally even though the adult's functional cavity is a blood-filled *hemocoel* — the bank still scores them true-coelom.)
- **Pseudocoelom:** cavity present but *not fully mesoderm-lined* — **nematodes (C. elegans) = the go-to distractor.**
- **Acoelom / none:** cnidarians — diploblastic, no mesoderm at all. **Jellyfish = NO.**

The bee-vs-jellyfish-vs-C.-elegans trio is a stock question: answer is bee only.

cards.title: Buzz words → instant recall
cards.body:
- **nematocyst / cnidocyte / man o' war / sea anemone** → **Cnidaria** (radial, diploblastic, no coelom)
- **choanocyte / spongocyte / collar cell / spicule / spongin** → **Porifera** (most basal, no true tissues)
- **blastopore → mouth** → protostome; **blastopore → anus** → deuterostome
- **spiral, determinate cleavage** → protostome; **radial, indeterminate** → deuterostome
- **TMAO / spiral valve** → cartilaginous or basal fish (shark, ray, lungfish, sturgeon)
- **'contains' / 'nested within'** → clade-hierarchy question — check the DIRECTION (bigger holds smaller)
- **amniotic egg** in an ordering item → the LAST/most-derived trait

cards.title: Worked buzz — TMAO fish
cards.body:
*Clue:* 'A fish makes extensive TMAO. Which are true: has a lateral line; has jaws; is ovoviviparous?'

**Land it fast:** TMAO (trimethylamine oxide) is the osmolyte that counteracts urea toxicity and high-pressure protein destabilization — the signature of **sharks/rays and deep-sea fishes** (chondrichthyans).
- **Lateral line?** Yes — *all* fishes have one.
- **Jaws?** Yes — sharks are gnathostomes.
- **Ovoviviparous?** Yes — common in sharks (eggs retained, hatch internally).

So the answer is **ALL**. One buzz-signal (TMAO → shark) unlocks all three.

cards.title: Worked buzz — 'contains' direction
cards.body:
*Clue:* 'Which pairs have the first group containing the second? (1) Echinodermata & Asteroidea (2) Protostomia & Bilateria (3) Pancrustacea & Myriapoda'

**Rule:** the *larger* clade holds the *smaller*.
- (1) Echinodermata **contains** Asteroidea (starfish) — TRUE.
- (2) Protostomia & Bilateria — Bilateria is the *huge* clade holding BOTH protostomes and deuterostomes, so Protostomia can't contain it — **FALSE** (reversed).
- (3) Pancrustacea (crustaceans + insects/hexapods) does NOT contain Myriapoda — myriapods branch separately in Arthropoda — FALSE.

Answer: **1 only.** Always ask 'which is bigger?' before saying yes.

cards.title: Classic distractor pairs the writers swap
cards.body:
- **Cleavage swap:** protostome = **spiral & determinate**, deuterostome = **radial & indeterminate**. 'Protostomes display radial cleavage' is a stock FALSE.
- **Coelom trap:** annelids/molluscs/arthropods/chordates = true coelom; **nematodes = PSEUDOcoelom**; cnidarians = none.
- **Containment reversal:** **Bilateria contains Protostomia**, never the reverse.
- **Tetrapod ≠ amniote:** amphibians are tetrapods but NOT amniotes — the #1 'which is false' chordate trap.
- **Deuterostomes are only 3 phyla** (Echinodermata, Chordata, **Hemichordata**). Hemichordata is the sneaky 'which is NOT a protostome' answer.
- **Starfish are deuterostomes**, not protostomes (they're echinoderms).

cards.title: Nested chordate clades
cards.body:
**Chordata ⊃ Craniata ⊃ Vertebrata ⊃ Gnathostomata ⊃ Tetrapoda ⊃ Amniota.** Each contains the next (this is the traditional morphological nesting the bank uses).

Every 'which chordate statement is false' question lives here:
- TRUE: all vertebrates are chordates; all gnathostomes are craniates; all mammals are tetrapods.
- FALSE: 'all tetrapods are amniotes' — amphibians break it.

Think of it as Russian dolls: the outer (bigger) clade always contains the inner. A statement of the form 'all X are Y' is true only when Y is the *larger* (outer) clade.

cards.title: Phylum-ID traps: wrong jelly, and 'sounds fake'
cards.body:
Two real traps on cell-type/phylum clues:

- **Wrong-jelly swap:** **Ctenophora** (comb jellies) is a real phylum but is the WRONG answer to sponge-cell clues. *Choanocytes / spongocytes / collar cells / spicules* → **Porifera**. Collar cells closely resemble **choanoflagellates**, the protist sister group of all animals — which is exactly why they flag the most *basal* animals (sponges), not comb jellies.
- **'Sounds obscure' is NOT a safe reject filter:** genuinely real phyla like **Placozoa, Loricifera, and Cycliophora** are things you've probably never heard of. Never eliminate an option just because the name is unfamiliar — reject on the *diagnostic trait*, not the vibe.

memorize.answer: Porifera (sponges — most basal, no true tissues)
Protostome (deuterostome = blastopore becomes the anus, mouth second)
Echinodermata, Chordata, Hemichordata (in Science Bowl, every other bilaterian phylum = protostome)
Mineralized skeleton → jaws → digited limbs → amniotic egg
Chordata ⊃ Craniata ⊃ Vertebrata ⊃ Gnathostomata ⊃ Tetrapoda ⊃ Amniota
Amphibians (tetrapods but lack the amniotic egg)
Pseudocoelom (not fully mesoderm-lined; jellyfish = none; bee = true coelom)
Cartilaginous/deep-sea fish (shark, ray) — counteracts urea toxicity & pressure damage
Basal fish intestine (sharks, rays, lungfish, sturgeons) — lost in teleosts and tetrapods
Cnidaria — it's outside Bilateria (diploblastic, radial); the others are all bilaterians

practice.note: Four-statement 'identify all true' about protostome development — every clause is a classic trap. Check each against the tree independently.
practice.solution: Answer is **1 only**. (1) TRUE — in protostomes the blastopore becomes the mouth. (2) FALSE — many protostomes (annelids, molluscs, arthropods) have a true coelom. (3) FALSE — protostomes show SPIRAL cleavage; radial is deuterostome. (4) FALSE — starfish are echinoderms, hence deuterostomes. Only statement 1 survives.

practice.note: 'Which is NOT a protostome?' — recall the short deuterostome list rather than testing each protostome.
practice.solution: Answer is **W) Hemichordata**. The deuterostomes are exactly three phyla — Echinodermata, Chordata, Hemichordata — so Hemichordata is the odd one out. Mollusca, Annelida, and Rotifera are all protostomes (Lophotrochozoa). Hemichordata is the sneaky deuterostome that shows up precisely because students forget it.

practice.note: True-coelom trio: honey bee, jellyfish, C. elegans. The whole item hinges on the coelom / pseudocoelom / none distinction.
practice.solution: Answer is **1 only**. Honey bee = eucoelomate (true coelom, mesoderm-lined; arthropods are classed as coelomates). Jellyfish = diploblastic, no mesoderm, so no coelom at all. C. elegans (a nematode) = PSEUDOcoelomate — a cavity, but not fully mesoderm-lined. Only the bee has a true coelom.

practice.note: 'Which chordate statement is FALSE' — pure clade-nesting logic. A statement 'all X are Y' is true only when Y is the larger/outer clade.
practice.solution: Answer is **Z) All tetrapods are amniotes** — FALSE, because amphibians are tetrapods but not amniotes. The others hold: vertebrates ⊂ chordates, gnathostomes ⊂ craniates, mammals ⊂ tetrapods (each smaller clade sits inside the larger one).

practice.note: Order the vertebrate traits by evolutionary appearance. Read them off the tree from fish toward amniotes.
practice.solution: Answer is **2, 3, 1**: mineralized skeleton (bone, early vertebrates) → limbs with digits (Tetrapoda) → amniotic egg (Amniota, most derived). The amniotic egg is last because it's the innovation that freed vertebrates from needing water to reproduce.

practice.note: TMAO fish — one buzz-signal (TMAO → shark/chondrichthyan) should unlock all three sub-statements.
practice.solution: Answer is **ALL**. TMAO marks a cartilaginous/deep-sea fish (shark or ray). (1) Lateral line — yes, all fishes have one. (2) Jaws — yes, sharks are gnathostomes. (3) Ovoviviparous — yes, common in sharks (eggs retained and hatch internally). All three are true.
