overview:
## What this covers

Science Bowl immunology is **not** the interleukin-soup you fear. Looking at the actual bank, the questions cluster into four tight buckets:

- **Innate vs. adaptive** — sorting cells/processes into the right arm (NK, mast, macrophage, neutrophil, dendritic, complement = innate; B cells, T cells, antibodies = adaptive).
- **Blood typing & Rh** — the single most-tested sub-area here (**4 of 10 questions**): ABO transfusion compatibility, Rh incompatibility → hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), and the Bombay-phenotype trap.
- **Antibodies (immunoglobulins)** — the five isotypes and their signature jobs, above all **IgG crossing the placenta**.
- **Techniques & clinical flags** — flow cytometry side scatter, hybridomas/monoclonals, antinuclear antibodies → lupus, "eat-me" signals.

## How it shows up

Half the questions are "identify all that apply" or ordering prompts — you don't get partial credit for knowing *most* of a category. The other half are single-fact MC recalls ("which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta?"). Both formats reward **automatic categorical reflexes**, not reasoning-from-scratch at the buzzer.

## The smartest way to learn it

Build **two tables cold**, then attach one mechanism to each specialty term:

1. **Innate vs. adaptive cell roster** — so any cell name sorts instantly.
2. **ABO/Rh compatibility grid** — universal donor O−, universal recipient AB+, and *you can receive blood lacking the antigen your plasma has antibodies against*.

Then bolt a *why* onto each oddball fact (why IgG and not IgM crosses the placenta; why phosphatidylserine flags a cell for eating; why NK cells are innate despite killing infected cells). Once the two tables are automatic, the whole topic collapses into fast recall.

cards.title: Innate vs. adaptive: the master split
cards.body:
**Innate = fast, non-specific, no memory.** Roster to memorize: **NK cells, mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, complement.**

**Adaptive = slow, specific, has memory.** Means **B cells, T cells, and antibodies** — anything with a *named lymphocyte* or a *specific antibody*.

**Fast sort rule:** if it involves a specific antibody or a named T/B lymphocyte → adaptive. If it's a granulocyte, a phagocyte, or a 'kills anything abnormal' cell → innate.

**Watch the bridge cells:** dendritic cells are *innate* but present antigen to T cells (they hand off to the adaptive arm), and the *classical* complement pathway is *triggered* by antibodies — the complement proteins themselves are still innate. A question naming complement or a dendritic cell wants 'innate.' This single split underlies the most-tested question type (identify-all-innate).

cards.title: WHY NK cells are innate (the #1 trap)
cards.body:
NK cells *feel* adaptive — they kill virus-infected and tumor cells, just like cytotoxic T cells. But they are **innate**.

**Mechanism (missing-self):** healthy cells display normal **MHC-I** = an 'I'm fine' signal. Cytotoxic T cells need to *see* antigen presented on MHC-I to kill. Infected/cancerous cells downregulate MHC-I to hide from T cells — and that *absent* signal is exactly what NK cells detect. They recognize **missing/abnormal self**, not a specific antigen.

No antigen specificity, no memory → innate. If a question describes killing infected cells *by detecting abnormal/absent surface proteins (low MHC-I)*, that's the NK-cell/innate giveaway (this is verbatim the classic distractor).

cards.title: WHY only IgG crosses the placenta
cards.body:
HDN and newborn passive immunity are **always IgG** — here's the mechanism:

- **IgG is a small monomer**, actively transported across the placenta via **FcRn receptors**. Small + a dedicated transporter = it crosses.
- **IgM is a huge pentamer** — far too big to cross, and it has no placental transporter. Mnemonic: **M = Massive / Mama-stays-out**. IgM is also the *first* antibody made in a response (another common ask).

So: passive immunity to the newborn = IgG; maternal anti-Rh antibodies that cause HDN = IgG; the pentamer that can't cross = IgM.

cards.title: The five immunoglobulin isotypes
cards.body:
Only IgG/IgM show up most, but 'most abundant' and 'allergy' questions probe the rest — anchor each to one job:

- **IgG** — most abundant in **serum/blood** (~75%); monomer; crosses placenta; opsonization + complement; dominates the *secondary* response.
- **IgM** — **pentamer**; *first* made (primary response); best complement activator; too big to cross the placenta.
- **IgA** — secretory **dimer**; guards **mucosa** (saliva, tears, breast milk, gut). It is the most *abundantly produced/secreted* isotype overall. Mnemonic: **A = mucosAl**.
- **IgE** — **allergy + parasites**; binds mast cells/basophils and triggers histamine release; *lowest* serum level. Mnemonic: **E = allergiEs**.
- **IgD** — sits on **naive B-cell** surfaces (with IgM); function largely unclear.

**The 'most abundant' trap:** *in serum* = **IgG**; *produced per day / in secretions* = **IgA**. Read which one the clue asks.

cards.title: The ABO/Rh compatibility grid
cards.body:
**Rule:** you can safely receive donor blood that **lacks the antigen your plasma has antibodies against.** You make antibodies against the A/B antigens you *don't* have.

- **O− = universal donor** (no A, B, or Rh antigens to attack).
- **AB+ = universal recipient** (no anti-A, anti-B, or anti-Rh antibodies).
- Worked example: a **B+ person** has anti-A antibodies, so they can take **B and O** (both lack A antigen), and Rh+ can take Rh+ or Rh−.

Only **donor RBC antigens** matter for packed cells — donor plasma antibodies are too dilute to count.

**Reversal trap:** for **plasma** transfusion the roles flip — **AB is the universal plasma donor** (no anti-A/anti-B) and **O the universal plasma recipient**. RBC rule and plasma rule are mirror images; a clue that says 'plasma' wants the flipped answer.

cards.title: Rh incompatibility → HDN
cards.body:
**Setup for hemolytic disease of the newborn: mother Rh−, father (and fetus) Rh+.**

- An Rh− mother sensitized by an Rh+ fetus makes **anti-Rh (anti-D) IgG**.
- Because **only IgG crosses the placenta**, those antibodies reach the *next* Rh+ fetus and hemolyze its RBCs — so the *first* Rh+ pregnancy usually sensitizes and *later* ones are affected.
- The father being Rh+ is what makes the fetus potentially Rh+.

**Answer pattern to lock in:** mother **negative**, father **positive** — never the reverse (the classic trap is picking the reverse).

cards.title: The Bombay 'O' trap
cards.body:
**Bombay phenotype = no H antigen.** The H antigen is the base sugar that the A- and B-enzymes decorate — no H means no A, B, *or* O antigen can be built (a Bombay patient has *no* ABO antigens on her RBCs).

The trap: students reflexively say 'O is universal, so give her O.' **Wrong.** Even type-O blood still displays the **H antigen**, and a Bombay patient's plasma has anti-A, anti-B, **AND anti-H** antibodies. So O triggers a hemolytic reaction too.

**Answer to 'who can donate — A/B/O/AB?': NONE.** A Bombay patient can only receive blood from another Bombay individual.

cards.title: Confusable pairs to keep straight
cards.body:
- **Phosphatidylserine vs. phosphatidylcholine** — apoptotic cells flip **PS** from the inner to the *outer* leaflet as the 'eat-me' signal macrophages recognize. PC/sphingomyelin/cholesterol are normal outer-leaflet residents → signal nothing.
- **Side scatter (SSC = granularity) vs. forward scatter (FSC = size)** — granulocytes win on SSC because they're packed with granules, not necessarily on FSC.
- **Diapedesis vs. margination vs. chemotaxis** — the full sequence is margination → rolling → adhesion → **diapedesis (crossing the vessel wall)** → chemotaxis. Diapedesis is *specifically* the crossing step (accept 'leukocyte extravasation'); this is exactly what these questions ask.
- **IgG vs. IgM** — IgG crosses placenta (small monomer, most abundant in serum); IgM does not (huge pentamer, first made).
- **RBC vs. plasma universal donor** — O− donates RBCs to anyone; AB donates *plasma* to anyone (mirror image).

cards.title: Buzz words → what to recall
cards.body:
- **'innate' / 'adaptive' / 'natural killer' / 'mast cell' / 'complement' / 'dendritic'** → immune-arm sorting (NK & mast & dendritic & complement = innate).
- **'Rh factor' / 'hemolytic disease of the newborn' / 'transfusion' / 'blood type' / 'Bombay'** → the ABO/Rh grid.
- **'immunoglobulin' / 'IgG/IgM' / 'cross the placenta' / 'passive immunity'** → antibody isotypes → **IgG**.
- **'most abundant antibody'** → **IgG in serum**, but **IgA if 'secretions/produced'**.
- **'allergy' / 'parasite' / 'binds mast cells'** → **IgE**.
- **'monoclonal antibody' / 'hybridoma'** → myeloma + B cell.
- **'flow cytometry' / 'side/forward scatter'** → SSC = granularity, order lymphocyte < monocyte < granulocyte.
- **'antinuclear antibodies (ANA)'** → **lupus (SLE)**.
- **'margination' then squeezing through vessel walls** → **diapedesis**.

cards.title: Worked buzz: the flow-cytometry ordering
cards.body:
**Clue:** 'Order T cell, monocyte, basophil by *increasing side scatter*.'

**Land it fast:** SSC = internal **granularity**, not size. 
- **T cell** = a lymphocyte, small and **agranular** → lowest SSC. 
- **Monocyte** = intermediate complexity → middle. 
- **Basophil** = a **granulocyte** packed with granules → highest SSC.

**Answer: 1, 2, 3 (T cell < monocyte < basophil).** The one-second version: 'lymphocyte < monocyte < granulocyte' for side scatter, every time. (If it said *forward* scatter you'd be judging size instead — and a large monocyte could outrank a granulocyte, so the order can change.)

cards.title: Clinical/technique one-hit facts
cards.body:
High-yield single-fact recalls that show up as MC:

- **Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) → Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.** ANA are autoantibodies against the cell's own nuclear contents (DNA, histones); ANA is the sensitive *screening* test for lupus.
- **Hybridoma = immortal myeloma cell fused with a B (plasma) cell → monoclonal antibodies.** A B cell makes one specific antibody but dies; myeloma is immortal but makes nothing useful — fuse them for an immortal antibody factory. The immune cell fused in is the **B cell**.
- **Mast cells release histamine** → vasodilation + increased vascular permeability = local inflammation/allergy; an **innate** process (and the effector step behind IgE-mediated allergy).

memorize.trigger: Immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta / causes HDN / gives newborn passive immunity
Immunoglobulin too big to cross the placenta / first antibody made in a response
Most abundant antibody in serum / blood
Antibody in mucosal secretions, saliva, tears, breast milk (secretory dimer)
Antibody mediating allergy and parasite defense; binds mast cells/basophils
Universal RBC donor / universal RBC recipient
memorize.answer: O− donor / AB+ recipient (for plasma it flips: AB donor / O recipient)

memorize.trigger: Bombay phenotype — which ABO types can donate to them
memorize.answer: NONE (only another Bombay; no H antigen, has anti-A, anti-B, anti-H)

memorize.trigger: NK cells — innate or adaptive, and how they detect targets
memorize.answer: Innate; detect missing/abnormal self (low MHC-I), no specific antigen

memorize.trigger: Neutrophils squeezing through gaps between endothelial cells (after margination)
'Eat-me' signal macrophages recognize on apoptotic cells
Hybridoma = myeloma cell fused with which immune cell
memorize.answer: B cell (plasma B cell) → monoclonal antibodies

memorize.trigger: Flow cytometry side scatter (SSC) measures / increasing-SSC order

memorize.answer: NK, mast, macrophage, neutrophil, dendritic, complement

practice.note: 'Identify all innate' — no partial credit. Sort each: antibodies and helper T cells are adaptive; NK (missing-self) and mast cells (histamine) are innate. Don't let NK 'killing infected cells' pull you toward adaptive.
practice.solution: Answer is 2 and 4. (1) B cells releasing antibodies = adaptive. (2) NK cells detecting abnormal surface proteins (low MHC-I) = innate, missing-self recognition. (3) Helper T cells releasing cytokines = adaptive. (4) Mast cells releasing histamine = innate inflammatory effector. Only 2 and 4 are innate.

practice.note: Pure isotype recall. The trigger words 'cross the placenta' and 'hemolytic disease of the newborn' both point to one answer.
practice.solution: IgG. It's a small monomer actively transported across the placenta via FcRn, giving newborn passive immunity and, when it's maternal anti-Rh, causing HDN. IgM (pentamer) is too big; IgA and IgD don't cross either.

practice.note: Get the direction right — the classic trap is reversing mother and father. Anchor on 'the mother must be the one making anti-Rh antibodies.'
practice.solution: Negative, Positive. An Rh− mother sensitized by an Rh+ fetus makes anti-Rh IgG; the father being Rh+ is what makes the fetus Rh+, giving the mother's IgG a target to hemolyze. So mother negative, father positive.

practice.note: Apply the grid to B+. She has anti-A antibodies, so any donor lacking the A antigen is safe; Rh+ can take Rh+ or Rh−. Check all three.
practice.solution: All. Jane is B+ (anti-A in plasma). (1) O− lacks A and any Rh antigen → safe. (2) O+ lacks A, and she's Rh+ so Rh+ is fine → safe. (3) B− lacks A, Rh− is fine for an Rh+ recipient → safe. None carry the A antigen her plasma attacks, so all three are compatible.

practice.note: The Bombay trap. Reflex 'O is universal' is wrong here — remember O blood still shows the H antigen, which Bombay plasma attacks.
practice.solution: NONE. Bombay phenotype has no H antigen and therefore has anti-A, anti-B, AND anti-H antibodies. Every normal ABO type — including O, which still displays H — would trigger a hemolytic reaction. Only another Bombay individual can donate, so none of A/B/O/AB is safe.

practice.note: Side scatter = granularity, not size. Rank by how many internal granules each cell has; a granulocyte must come last.
practice.solution: 1, 2, 3 (T cell < monocyte < basophil). SSC measures internal complexity/granularity. The T cell is a small agranular lymphocyte (lowest), the monocyte is intermediate, and the basophil is a granulocyte packed with granules (highest).

practice.note: Recall the two fusion partners of a hybridoma; the asked-for half is the antibody-producing immune cell.
practice.solution: B cell (plasma B cell). A hybridoma fuses an immortal myeloma cell (never dies but makes no useful antibody) with a B cell (makes one specific antibody but is mortal), yielding an immortal cell line that secretes a single monoclonal antibody.

subject: bio

why: At ~21.7% of the bio bank (75 of 346 questions), this is the single densest and highest-yield biology topic in Science Bowl — mastering its four buckets answers roughly one in five bio questions.
overview:
Molecular biology & biochemistry is the **densest topic in the bio bank** — about 1 in 5 bio questions (75/346). Don't try to memorize 75 loose facts; the whole topic collapses into **four buckets**, and almost every question announces which bucket it's in within the first clause.

- **Metabolism (~1/3 of all questions, the highest-leverage cluster):** glycolysis → Krebs (citric acid) cycle → electron transport / chemiosmosis, plus photosynthesis/Calvin cycle, beta-oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and shuttle systems. Know the *shape* of each pathway — what goes in, what comes out, which step does what — and you'll clear most of them.
- **Proteins & amino acids:** the four structure levels, polar vs nonpolar vs charged side chains, phosphorylation chemistry, and the recurring \"which substitution is most/least damaging\" framing.
- **DNA/RNA machinery:** replication (leading/lagging, topoisomerase, repair pathways), transcription/translation (codons, wobble, A→P→E sites, prokaryote vs eukaryote), and gene regulation (lac operon, miRNA/piRNA, transposons).
- **Lab techniques:** Western blot / SDS-PAGE, gel electrophoresis, PCR/qPCR, sequencing (Sanger, sequencing-by-synthesis, Nanopore), CRISPR, restriction cloning.

**How it shows up:** heavy on \"identify ALL that are true\" multi-select and \"order/rank these steps\" bonuses. Both reward *mechanism*, not vocab — you have to know *why* a fact is true to survive a partial-credit multi-select.

**Smartest prep:** draw the **central-dogma** flowchart and the **respiration + photosynthesis** flowcharts once from memory, then hang every fact on that scaffold. When a question starts, your first move is \"which of the four buckets?\" — that alone narrows the answer before you've heard the whole clue.

cards.title: The respiration highway: glycolysis → Krebs → ETC
cards.body:
Memorize the pathway as a **conveyor belt** with a signature enzyme/molecule per stage:

- **Glycolysis** — glucose gets phosphorylated by **hexokinase** (traps glucose in the cell by slapping on a charged phosphate it can't diffuse back out with). Cytosol. Net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
- **Krebs / citric acid cycle** — makes **citrate**; the two CO2-releasing (oxidative-decarboxylation) steps produce **α-ketoglutarate** then **succinyl-CoA**. The **succinyl-CoA → succinate** step is the cycle's **substrate-level phosphorylation** (makes GTP/ATP directly, no O2 needed). Matrix.
- **Electron transport chain** — reduces then re-oxidizes **cytochrome c**, pumps protons, makes the bulk of ATP via chemiosmosis. Inner membrane.

The classic ordering bonus is **phosphorylation → citrate → cyt c**. Respiration overall is **catabolic and exergonic** (breaks down, releases energy). Same-name traps: Krebs = TCA = tricarboxylic acid cycle, all three accepted.

cards.title: WHY the lagging strand is discontinuous (and why chemiosmosis makes heat)
cards.body:
Two mechanisms that unlock a cluster of questions:

**Lagging strand:** ALL DNA polymerases extend **only 5'→3'** (they add nucleotides onto a free 3'-OH). The two template strands run antiparallel, so one daughter strand can be made continuously toward the fork (leading) but the other must be built in **backward chunks = Okazaki fragments** pointing away from the fork. "Discontinuous / 5'→3' / Okazaki" all describe the lagging strand. **Topoisomerase/gyrase** relieves the supercoiling ahead of the fork (quinolones hit bacterial gyrase = topo II; camptothecin hits topo I).

**Uncoupling:** The ETC pumps protons to build a gradient that ATP synthase cashes in. **Brown fat's UCP1 (thermogenin)** lets protons leak back *without* passing through ATP synthase — the energy dissipates as **heat**. So an uncoupled mitochondrion keeps burning O2 (**O2 consumption stays high or rises** as the ETC races to rebuild the leaking gradient) but **ATP output drops**.

cards.title: WHY these buzz answers are forced by chemistry
cards.body:
Don't memorize the answer — memorize the reason, so distractors can't fool you:

- **SDS-PAGE separates by size only** *because* SDS coats every protein with uniform negative charge, swamping the protein's own charge, and heat/reductant unfolds it. Corollary: it **can't** distinguish same-size residues (Leu vs Ile) or resolve native charge/shape.
- **Gel filtration (size-exclusion): big elutes FIRST** — large molecules can't enter the porous beads, so they take the short path around; small ones get trapped in pores and lag. Tetrameric **hemoglobin elutes before monomeric myoglobin**.
- **Phosphomimetic = Glu/Asp** — phosphorylation adds negative charge, and Glu/Asp are the naturally negative residues, so they stand in for phospho-Ser/Thr/Tyr and lock an enzyme in its "phosphorylated" state.
- **AZT hits anything using reverse transcriptase** — it's a chain-terminating thymidine analog (no 3'-OH), so it blocks HIV RT, LINE retrotransposons, AND telomerase (which is itself an RT).

cards.title: Central dogma machinery: codons, wobble, ribosome sites
cards.body:
- **61 sense codons** code amino acids ($64 - 3$ stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA). Watch the trap: it's 61 *codons*, but far **fewer tRNAs** (~30–40 in a cell) — wobble lets one tRNA read several codons, so "number of tRNAs = 61" is wrong.
- **AUG = methionine = start codon.**
- Ribosome sites run **A → P → E** (Aminoacyl enters, Peptidyl holds the growing chain, Exit deacylated tRNA). **Peptidyl transferase** — a **ribozyme in the large (50S in prokaryotes) subunit** — forms peptide bonds; macrolides target it.
- **Wobble:** the **3rd codon position** is flexible, letting one tRNA read several codons. **Inosine (from deaminated adenine; base = hypoxanthine)** in the wobble position reads U, C, and A.
- mRNA first binds the **small ribosomal subunit** in both pro- and eukaryotes.

cards.title: Photosynthesis: RuBisCO, RuBP, and where water's electrons go
cards.body:
- **RuBisCO** — the **most abundant protein on Earth** — fixes CO2. The **first Calvin step reacts CO2 with the 5-carbon sugar RuBP**, making an unstable 6C that immediately splits into two 3C (3-PGA). "Most abundant protein / fixes carbon onto RuBP" is *always* RuBisCO.
- **Calvin cycle location: stroma**, NOT the thylakoid lumen (common distractor). Its direct product is G3P, not glucose.
- **Light reactions:** electrons from **splitting water end up in NADPH** (water → PSII →... → PSI → NADP+). O2 is the waste byproduct.
- **Proton topology trap:** chloroplast ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane and protons are pumped **INTO the thylakoid lumen** (opposite direction from the mitochondrial intermembrane space) — the gradient flows lumen → stroma.
- Oxidizing-strength order: NAD+ < cytochrome c < **P680+** (the strongest oxidant in biology — strong enough to rip electrons off water).
- **C4 and CAM plants** modify carbon *capture* (spatially or temporally concentrating CO2) to avoid photorespiration; the Calvin cycle itself is unchanged.

cards.title: Buzz words → instant answers
cards.body:
When you hear the clue, fire the answer before the sentence ends:

- "Most abundant protein / fixes CO2 onto RuBP" → **RuBisCO**
- "Fluoroacetate / citrate builds up" → **aconitase** (fluorocitrate blocks it); "Krebs intermediate made alongside CO2" → **α-ketoglutarate**
- "Toroidal / plectonemic supercoils, quinolone / camptothecin" → **topoisomerase (gyrase)**
- "Coats proteins with uniform negative charge" → **SDS**
- "Viral load quantification" → **(RT-)qPCR**; "protein sequencing by mass" → **tandem mass spec**
- "Peptide-bond-forming enzyme in the large subunit / a ribozyme" → **peptidyl transferase**
- "AZT / azidothymidine" → chain-terminates **reverse transcriptase** (HIV, retrotransposons, telomerase)
- "Uncouples / brown fat / thermogenin" → proton leak, **heat not ATP**
- "Chemically similar to phenylalanine, gets phosphorylated on the insulin receptor" → **tyrosine**

cards.title: The distractor pairs they deliberately swap
cards.body:
These are engineered traps — questions pair the *wrong* member on purpose:

- **Base excision vs nucleotide excision:** nucleotide excision removes **bulky lesions** (UV thymine dimers); base excision removes a **single damaged base** (uracil, hypoxanthine) via a glycosylase. Double-strand break → **homologous recombination** (or NHEJ). Match by damage *size*.
- **Retrotransposon (copy-paste, RNA intermediate + RT) vs DNA transposon (cut-paste, transposase).** **LINEs = retrotransposons**, silenced by **piRNA**.
- **T state = Tense = low O2 affinity** vs **R = Relaxed = high**. A **left-shifted** curve is high affinity = R, not T.
- **Sequencing-by-synthesis (Sanger, Illumina — builds a complementary strand) vs Nanopore (reads the intact strand directly by ionic current — NOT by synthesis).**
- **Circular dichroism = secondary structure (α-helix vs β-sheet), NOT size.** SDS-PAGE, gel filtration, and density centrifugation size proteins; CD does not.
- **Hb iron coordinates to the proximal histidine, not aspartate.**

cards.title: Amino-acid substitution damage: rank by how much chemistry changes
cards.body:
"Which mutation hurts most/least" is a repeat favorite. Score each swap by **size + polarity + charge** change — the smaller the total change, the more conservative:

- **Least damaging (conservative): Met → Val** — both nonpolar/hydrophobic, no charge introduced (Leu↔Ile is the textbook example of the same idea).
- **Most damaging:** nonpolar → charged/polar, e.g. **Val → Asp** (nonpolar → negatively charged) or **Trp → Asn** (big hydrophobic → polar). Val→Asp buried in myoglobin disrupts 1°, 2°, AND 3° structure — but **not quaternary**, because myoglobin is a monomer.
- **Buried in a membrane / hydrophobic core?** Pick the **most hydrophobic** residue: **tryptophan** beats Tyr or Thr. (Tyr's ring carries a polar –OH; Thr is polar/hydroxylated — both unfavorable in a lipid core.)

Every amino acid shares a **backbone carboxyl + amino group**; thiol (Cys) and hydroxyl (Ser/Thr/Tyr) are side-chain-specific.

cards.title: Worked buzz: the malate–aspartate shuttle
cards.body:
**Clue heard:** "To move electrons from cytosolic NADH made in glycolysis into the ETC, malate is imported into the matrix coupled with the export of what intermediate formed from transamination of oxaloacetate?"

**How you land it fast:**
1. Bucket check → **metabolism**, specifically "getting glycolytic NADH's electrons into the mitochondrion." That's the **malate–aspartate shuttle** (NADH itself can't cross the inner membrane).
2. The keyword is **transamination of oxaloacetate** — adding an amino group to the OAA keto-acid backbone. OAA + amino group = **aspartate**.
3. Answer: **aspartate.**

The trick is recognizing that "OAA + transamination" is a one-step chemical transformation (keto acid → its amino acid), not a whole pathway to trace out.

cards.title: Gene regulation & mobile elements
cards.body:
- **lac operon** gene order from the operator: **lacZ, lacY, lacA** (Z closest, so rank prompts want Z→Y→A). Z = β-galactosidase, Y = permease, A = transacetylase.
- **Max lac expression: high lactose, low glucose** — lactose (as allolactose) removes the repressor AND low glucose raises cAMP so CAP/CRP activates transcription. Glucose present = catabolite repression = low expression even with lactose.
- **Retrotransposons copy-and-paste via an RNA intermediate** (LINEs, using reverse transcriptase); DNA transposons cut-and-paste via transposase.
- **Epigenetic activation** = remove DNA methylation OR add histone acetylation (both loosen/open chromatin).
- Eukaryotic translation regulated by **miRNA** (imperfect base-pairing → repression/degradation); one mRNA read simultaneously by many ribosomes = **polyribosome (polysome)**.

cards.title: Prokaryote vs eukaryote: the one-line discriminators
cards.body:
Multi-select bonuses hammer these contrasts. Keep the discriminators ready:

- **"Transcription and translation happen simultaneously"** → **prokaryote only** (no nucleus; eukaryotic mRNA must be processed and exit the nucleus first).
- **Polycistronic mRNA** (one transcript → multiple proteins) → prokaryote (operons).
- Both: mRNA first binds the **small ribosomal subunit**; both synthesize protein **N→C** and read mRNA **5'→3'**.
- **Signal peptides** sit at the **N-terminus and get cleaved** during maturation → true for **secreted/membrane-processed** proteins (preproinsulin, angiotensinogen), NOT cytosolic ones (hexokinase, calmodulin).
- **PCR denaturation** breaks the **hydrogen bonds** between strands (the covalent phosphodiester backbone must survive — that's what you're copying).

memorize.trigger: Most abundant protein on Earth / fixes CO2 onto RuBP
Krebs intermediate produced alongside a CO2
Electrons from splitting water end up in…
Coats proteins with uniform negative charge (so SDS-PAGE sorts by size only)
Enzyme that forms peptide bonds, a ribozyme in the large subunit
Number of sense codons coding amino acids
memorize.answer: 61 (64 minus 3 stops) — but fewer tRNAs, thanks to wobble
Reverse transcriptase — so HIV, retrotransposons, and telomerase

memorize.trigger: Technique that CANNOT size proteins (reports secondary structure)
Insulin-receptor residue phosphorylated, chemically like phenylalanine
Malate–aspartate shuttle: intermediate exported from the matrix
Krebs step that does substrate-level phosphorylation (makes GTP/ATP directly)

practice.note: Krebs 'which intermediate is made alongside CO2' — a repeat toss-up. The two carbon-losing (oxidative-decarboxylation) steps are isocitrate→α-KG and α-KG→succinyl-CoA. Citrate and isocitrate come BEFORE any CO2 is released; oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end without a CO2 at that step. Among the choices, only α-KG qualifies.
practice.solution: Alpha-ketoglutarate. Isocitrate is oxidatively decarboxylated to α-ketoglutarate, releasing the first CO2 of the cycle — so α-KG is the listed intermediate produced alongside that CO2. Citrate and isocitrate precede decarboxylation; oxaloacetate is regenerated without an accompanying CO2 at its step.

practice.note: lac operon gene order from the operator. The prompt lists them scrambled (lacA, lacY, lacZ) and wants closest→furthest. Reflex: Z, Y, A from the operator.
practice.solution: Order is 3, 2, 1 (lacZ, then lacY, then lacA). Transcription proceeds from the promoter/operator through lacZ (β-galactosidase) first, then lacY (permease), then lacA (transacetylase) — so lacZ is closest to the operator and lacA furthest.

practice.note: Which residues are stable in a hydrophobic membrane core — multi-select, so evaluate each. Tyrosine has a polar –OH on its ring; threonine is polar/hydroxylated. Only the fully nonpolar aromatic survives.
practice.solution: 3 only (tryptophan). A residue buried in the membrane's lipid core must be hydrophobic. Tryptophan's large nonpolar indole side chain is stable there; tyrosine carries a polar hydroxyl and threonine is a polar hydroxylated residue, so both are unfavorable in a hydrophobic environment.

practice.note: 'Which technique CANNOT distinguish proteins by size' — the CD trap. Gel filtration, SDS-PAGE, and density centrifugation all sort by size/mass; circular dichroism reports secondary structure instead.
practice.solution: Circular dichroism. CD measures differential absorption of left- vs right-circularly-polarized light to assess secondary-structure content (α-helix vs β-sheet), giving no size information. Gel filtration, SDS-PAGE, and density centrifugation all separate or sort molecules by size/mass, so CD is the odd one out.

practice.note: AZT multi-select. Recognize AZT as a chain-terminating thymidine analog (lacks a 3'-OH) that poisons reverse transcriptase — then ask which of the three listed processes uses an RT.
practice.solution: ALL. Azidothymidine is incorporated by reverse transcriptase and, lacking a 3'-OH, terminates chain elongation. HIV replication, retrotransposon (copy-and-paste) duplication, and telomere extension by telomerase all depend on a reverse-transcriptase activity, so AZT inhibits every one.

practice.note: Malate–aspartate shuttle. The tell is 'transamination of oxaloacetate' — adding an amino group to the OAA keto-acid backbone. Don't overthink it as a pathway; it's a one-step keto-acid→amino-acid conversion.
practice.solution: Aspartate. The malate–aspartate shuttle moves reducing equivalents from cytosolic NADH into the matrix: malate enters and is oxidized back to oxaloacetate, which is transaminated to aspartate for export. Transamination of the α-keto acid oxaloacetate yields the amino acid aspartate.

subject: bio
